WEDNESDAY, 12 DECEMBER 2012
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m.
Prayers.
Economic Programme—Progress
1. TODD McCLAY (National—Rotorua)  to the Minister of Finance : What
progress has the Government made with its economic programme in 2012?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associ ate Minister of Finance) on behalf of the Minister
of Finance : The Government is making very good progress in the face of very
significant ongoing global economic challenges. The Government was re-elected with a
clear plan to build a faster -growing economy that can enc ourage businesses to invest
and grow. We are focused on four main  priorities: responsibly manage the
Government’s finances so we can return to  surplus and repay debt, push ahead with a
wide-ranging programme of microeconomic re form to create a more productive and
competitive economy, drive better results and better value from public services, and
support the rebuild of our second -largest city after its eart hquakes. New Zealanders can
be reassured that this Government is abso lutely focused on creating more opportunities
to grow the economy, unlike the Greens-Labour Opposition, which is constantly—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Order!

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: What progress is the Government making with responsibly managing
its finances so it can return to surplus, start repaying debt, and build a buffer against
future shocks?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Once again, the Government is making very good progress.
On coming into office in late 2008, the Government was presented with forecasts
showing permanent structural deficits a nd ever-increasing Government debt. This
Government has worked hard to turn that  situation round by reining in new spending
and reprioritising existing spending to deliver better results, and that is all despite the
extra costs that have come from the Ca nterbury earthquakes. The Crown’s operating
deficit before gains and losses was $9.2 billion in the year ended June 2012—half of the
$18.4 billion in the previous year—and the late st forecast will be included in the Half
Year Economic and Fiscal Update next Tues day. The Government ha s set a target of
returning to surplus in 2014-15. That is very important so that we can reduce debt to
more prudent levels and build resilience to future shocks.

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: What approach is the Governme nt taking in building a more
productive and competitive economy?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Government is working aggressively to do everything
to give businesses the confid ence to invest, grow, and crea te jobs. The Government has
taken a wide range of measures to ensure economic growth is built on a solid foundation
of exports, savings, and productive investment. The programme that we are undertaking
is set out in the Business Growth Agenda, which contains more than 250 initiatives for
expanding our export markets, encouragi ng innovation, developing skills, building
infrastructure, improving our natural resour ce use, and growi ng capital markets.
Together they are a comprehensive agenda  of microeconomic reform, which will
support jobs and assist businesses to become more internationally competitive.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Before I call the honourable memb er, the House is unacceptably
noisy. But I remind Ministers that if they go on with very long answers—[ Interruption]
Order! If they go on with very long answers the House will tend to get restive.
7456 Questions for Oral Answer 12 Dec 2012

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: What reports has he received on  proposals that would put the New
Zealand economy at risk, cost thousands  of jobs, and increase the country’s
vulnerability to overseas lenders?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I have seen many such propos als this year. They include
saying no to responsible mining, saying no to making movies in this country, saying no
to seabed exploration for oil and gas, sa ying no to a convention centre in Auckland,
saying no to speeding up the Resource Management Act, saying no to the Government’s
multibillion-dollar investment in roads and other infrastructure, saying yes to a capital
gains tax and more costs on business, saying yes to printing mone y, and saying yes to
constantly talking down the New Zealand economy. That economic prescription would
cost thousands of jobs. It is called voodoo economics, and it  is what the Green-Labour
Opposition wants for New Zealand.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: After 4 years as Minister of Fi nance, what does the Minister of

items.speaker: Finance regard as his greatest failure
items.text: unempl oyment at its highest in 13 years, income
inequality at its highest recorded level, 54,000 people leaving for Au stralia in the past
year, 270,000 children living in poverty, a current account deficit forecast by the IMF to
be the worst in the developed world, a widening wage gap with Australia, negative
household savings, or external non-Government  debt at 100 perc ent of GDP? I will
accept the answer: “All of the above.”

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I think the member has inadvertently laid out exactly why
the Labour Party is not trusted to be the G overnment of New Zealand. Most of the stuff
he said was completely wrong and most of the stuff he said was actually worse under
the Labour Government, including the balance of payments. And he has the cheek to sit
there and pretend the global financial crisis did not happen and that the Government has
not faced the Christchurch earthquakes. As long as he stay s on “Planet Labour”, he will
stay over there on “Planet Opposition Benches”.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I know it is the last day of class, but the House is just too noisy. It is
no particular member’s fault. There is no way I could stop a lengt hy question, because
we have had a lot of lengthy answers. What I ask members to be mindful of is that we
should not have too long questions and we should not have too long answers, and we
just need to be a little more reasonable with interjections.
Ministers—Performance of Ministers of Finance and Education
2. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by his promise to New Zealanders th at “I expect high standards from my
Ministers … if they don’t meet the standard s I set then obviously I will take action if
necessary”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Has Bill English, the Minister of Finance, met the standards that
he sets, given that the number of une mployed New Zealanders has risen by 78,000
under his watch?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes. As the Associate Minister  of Finance has just pointed
out, we are dealing with a gl obal financial crisis, we have  created 65,000 jobs over the
last 3 years, and the New Zealand economy is more productive.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he consider it acceptable that unemployment is rising in
New Zealand while it is falling in our major trading partners, and does that not point to
a failed economic policy from him and his Ministers?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: In relation to the last part, no, and in relation to the first part,
in many of those countries the unemployment ra te started at a lot higher level. On that
basis, if you go and have a look at what has happened in terms of the unemployment
12 Dec 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 7457
benefit, this is a Government that has got 49,000 people on an unemployment benefit—
a lot lower. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I want to hear this question.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does it not come down to this: Bill English has failed to create
the conditions that lead to job growth, peopl e are losing jobs here while the job market
is improving in other countries, and it is only record emigration to Australia that is
preventing unemployment reaching even higher levels?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: How did his education Minister  meet his high standards when
she unlawfully decided to close Salisbury School for disabled girls?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: What is true is that the cour ts have ruled that it is not
appropriate to go forward, on the basis of safe ty. It is also true that the Minister
thoroughly considered that issue. The Minister never considered having a coeducational
school. She considered having a school that wa s co-located, and it is yet to be seen
whether that transpires.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Before I call the member, can I say to the Labour front-benchers
that when another party is asking a question, it has a right to hear the answer. Some
courtesy is reasonable.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The question asked how
the Minister met his high standards, and he gave us a recitation of  the facts, which is
fine, but what is of concern are the standards. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am on my feet, I say to  the National back-benchers. The
member will recollect that in his question he asked how the Minister met certain high
standards, and then made an assertion of fact in his question, about a decision being
unlawful. The Prime Minister dealt with that assertion of fact in answering, which he is
perfectly entitled to do.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he think that it meet s the standards of New Zealand
parents, let alone the Prime Minister, that his education Minister decided to close
Salisbury School and send girls with intellec tual disabilities to  a boys’ school where
their risk of sexual abuse would be seven tim es higher, and did she not think that the
danger she was putting those girls into was her responsibility?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: A number of the assumptions  the member has made are
factually incorrect. What was proposed was co-locating—effectively, single-sex schools
on the same site. It is an idea that has a lot of merit.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Putting aside the unlawfulness of  the Minister’s action, does a
Minister who blatantly disregards evidence a bout the safety of the most vulnerable girls
and who abrogates her responsibility to consid er their safety, and who, according to the
High Court, does not even think the safety  of schoolkids is her business—does that
Minister still meet high standards?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: In relation to the last part, yes. In relation to the first part, the
member is making all sorts of assumptions th at are not correct. The Minister actually
thoroughly considered the issue of safety, and that issue was thoroughly discussed.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: How can New Zealand parents have confidence in the safety of
their kids at school when his education Mi nister takes actions that she knows will
expose children to increased risk of sexual a nd physical violence, according to the High
Court judgment that found her actions illegal?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member is just totally and utterly wrong, basically.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I seek leave to table the High Court judgment that shows that
his Minister is totally wrong.
7458 Questions for Oral Answer 12 Dec 2012

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The document is a public documen t. Because of the controversy,
though, I will seek the leave of the House. L eave is sought to table that document. Is
there any objection? There is objection.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does it not boil down to this: He kia Parata is the person who is
ultimately responsible for the safety of ch ildren at school, and she has displayed a
blatant disregard for the safety of her child ren, and does not that make her unfit to be a
Minister of Education?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, and no.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Will he be writing to the parents of Salisbury School to explain
to them why he continues to have confidence in a Minister of Education who, according
to the High Court, unlawfully acted to put th eir children at greater risk of sexual and
physical abuse?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, it is not my intention to do so.
Prime Minister—Statements and Confidence in Ministers’ Statements
3. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by all his statements and have confidence in the statements of all his Ministers?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I will start by wishing the Leader of the
Opposition a merry Christmas. Yes, I stand by all my statements. I have confidence in
all my Ministers. Although it may have b een the case that Ministers in a previous
Government had to run their statements past their Prime Minister, I do not run such an
autocratic Government. I can only have confidence in those statements I have
specifically seen or heard.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: I return the compliments to the Prime Minister. Does he stand by his
statement that “Yep, in the end, you know , we need to. We need to get that
unemployment rate down, and th at’s whatever we think of the merits or robustness of
the number. We need to be printing a lowe r number.”, and when will he be printing a
lower number?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am reasonably confident it will be before the next election.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he stand by his statement that  this year has been much more
business as usual, and is an additiona l 19,000 people unemployed over the last year
business as usual?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: To the first bit, yes.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he stand by his answer in response to Labour’s claims of
increased migration to Australia that “Yep, they’ve got a point, but, I mean, it’s a fine
kind of conundrum in a way because we star ted that argument, so I’m not arguing the
merits.”, and how does he reconcile this answ er with his statement that this year has
been much more about business as usual?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am simply making the point that a strong Australia has some
real merits for New Zealand. It is the larg est source of tourists  to New Zealand, the
largest source of our exports, and the largest sour ce of foreign investment, so a very
weak Australia does not actually help New Zealand. But, ye s, I stand by the view that
we want New Zealanders to stay here if they can.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he agree with his finance Minister that “child poverty rates fell
in working families from around 16 percent to 8 percent,” from 2004 to 2007, the period
in which Working for Families was rolled out, and how many children have his tax cuts
helped out of poverty, given that hardship ra tes for children have risen from 16 percent
to 21 percent in the last 4 years?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I simply cannot verify the fact s of the last bit, because we
know that they are typically unreliable when they come from Labour. If we look at the
first, yes, it is true that Working for Families had a benefit in assisting children in
12 Dec 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 7459
poverty. That is true. It is  also true that when La bour had 3 years—2005, 2006, and
2007—where the combined surpluses were $20 billion, there were still 240,000 children
in New Zealand in poverty. The simple bottom line was it did not care enough to do
much about it.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Given that over the last year th ere have been an additional 19,000
unemployed, a record 54,000 people leaving fo r Australia, and inequality rising to the
highest level ever, and that the rate of children living in hardship has risen by 40 percent
since 2007, does he stand by his statement that the low point for him was his inability to
sell New Zealand’s assets?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, that was one of the low points. There were a couple of
others; that was one of them. The good news is we comprehensively won that court case
yesterday.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Question No. 4, Nicky Wagner. [ Interruption] Order! I want to be
able to hear Nicky Wagner. Question No. 4.
Canterbury, Recovery—Community Engagement, Cost, and Commentary
4. NICKY WAGNER (National—Christchurch Central)  to the Minister for

items.speaker: Canterbury Earthquake Recovery
items.text: How is the Government delivering a strong and
effective recovery for greater Christchurch following the earthquakes?
The Government is doing its part to deliver a strong and effective recovery by working
through the Canterbury Earthqu ake Recovery Authority, w ith the community at the
heart of the vision, as expre ssed in the recovery strate gy published in May of 2011. As
the strategy states, community engagement is key to a successful  recovery. We are
working extensively with our communities to  deliver best results , mindful that timely,
clear, and decisive decision -making is essential to re covery. The Government has
committed considerable resources to implem enting a strong, effective recovery. Known
costs to date total $13 billion, with more decisions to be made. The arms of Government
at all levels have been involved, and are work ing tirelessly to delive r on this recovery
for the people of Greater Christchurch, de spite the best efforts of many Opposition
politicians.

items.speaker: Nicky Wagner
items.text: What has been the fiscal cost of the Canterbury earthquakes?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: The cost will consolidate across many categories, and
some of the features of that cost will be  $2.5 billion for the repair of the horizontal
infrastructure, with $500 million spent by the end of this year. Widespread acceptance
of the Crown offer by homeowners in the re sidential red zones ha s meant that over $1
billion has been spent in paying out 5,212 se ttlements so far. Land zoning decisions
mean that red zone offers will have a gr oss cost to the Crown exceeding $1.9 billion.
The Earthquake Commission has now paid out in  excess of $4 billion; nearly $1 billion
of that has been funded. Over 28,000 homes have been repaired by the Fletcher EQR
project team. The total Earthquake Commission payout will be $12 billion, with over $7
billion coming from Crown funds. The final cost  is not yet known. We know that it will
cost the Government somewhere in excess of  $13 billion, but the total economic cost is
likely to be about $30 billi on. I know that the people of  Greater Christchurch are
grateful for that and sick and tired of the negative rubbish they get—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. If the Minister was
capable of answering that que stion properly, he would have  taken far less time. He is
just wasting the House’s time now. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! The Leader of the House should know
better than to interject on a point of orde r. Ministers are taking a long time to answer
questions from their own colleagues. That will  inevitably lead to more noise in the
7460 Questions for Oral Answer 12 Dec 2012
House, and it is not that he lpful. Answers to questions should be reasonably brief.
[Interruption] Order!

items.speaker: Hon Lianne Dalziel
items.text: Has he heard none of the concerns that have come from the
people of Christchurch who have been affected by the Government’s top-down recovery
process, many of these concerns having been summed up in this book, The Christchurch
Fiasco; and will he describe its author, who lives in West Melton, as another enemy of
the recovery, as he did the Press?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I listen to thousands of pe ople in Canterbury who are
very, very satisfied with the way things are going forward. If I had listened to some of
the commentary coming to us—allegedly in the name of people who are upset—from
Opposition politicians, we would be a long way further behind than we are at the
present time. There will be people who will write books and have views, but, in the end,
if we stop making decisions and stop doing th ings, we will stop things happening. That
is what the Labour Opposition wants.

items.speaker: Hon Lianne Dalziel
items.text: I seek leave to table The Christchurch Fiasco: The Insurance
Aftershock and its Implications for New Zealand and Beyond, by first-time author Sarah
Miles.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?
There is objection.

items.speaker: Hon Lianne Dalziel
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Sorry, I think the
Minister—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] No, order! What is the point of order about?
Leave was sought and I heard a member clearly deny leave, a nd that is the end of that
matter.

items.speaker: Hon Lianne Dalziel
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. A comment was made
about the author by one of the members, and I take exception—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! That is irre levant. Members are at
liberty to comment on authors so long as it is  not—the member is absolutely at liberty
to comment on authors.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Describing someone as a
loopy nutter across the House is just—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Now, look—[ Interruption] Order! Look, someone will—
even if it is the last day, I will not hesita te if the House does not show a little more
respect for this place. That  point of order was totally  unnecessary. Members have
referred to people outside this House by worse terms than that, and—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: No, it was a person outside—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That will be the end of this nonsense. On the last day,
members can show a little better sense.
David Bain—Binnie Report on Compensation Claim and Peer Review of Report
5. CHARLES CHAUVEL (Labour)  to the Minister of Justice : What are the
specific “assumptions” based on “inco rrect facts” demonstrating some
“misunderstanding of New Zealand law” that sh e alleges are contained in the report of
Justice Binnie concerning the application by Mr Bain for compensation for wrongful
conviction and imprisonment?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: I stated in my media release that
“My concerns are broadly that the report appeared to contain assumptions based on
incorrect facts, and showed a misunderstand ing of New Zealand la w.” Prior to giving
examples, I need to give just a little bit of context to this. I can advise the House that an
independent peer review of the first Bi nnie advice is being done by the Hon Robert
Fisher QC, and I am consider ing the public request made by  Mr Bain’s supporters to
12 Dec 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 7461
release both these reports—or advice to me—before Cabinet has made its decision. One
of the things I am considering is whether or not it is going to be in Mr Bain’s interests
or in the interests of justice to do so. But in relation to the examples sought, there are
many. I will give the House two of those. The first is relying on incorrect understanding
of what has been given in evidence. In th is case, Justice Binnie asserts that a named
scientist testified at the first trial that he had chemically enhanced the prints and later
sought to resile from this. The reference to chemical e nhancement was an error on a
label attached to a fingerprint, and this was explained as such by the named scientist at
the retrial. A second example is in relation to assumptions as to the correctness of
submissions on the law. Justice Binnie appe ars to have assumed to be correct Mr
Karam’s submission that the adverse infere nces should be drawn against the Crown
case on the basis of evid ence that is no longer available. This is incompatible with the
onus of proof being on Mr Bain in this particular case, because this is, in fact, a request
for Cabinet to use its discretion, and that is very clearly wrong.

items.speaker: Charles Chauvel
items.text: Having summarised some of her criticisms of Justice Binnie’s
report, why does she not simply release it in full so that the taxpayers, who have already
paid over $400,000 for it, can asse ss for themselves whether those criticisms are fair; or
is the prospect of dropping it in the press gall ery just before Christmas in the hope of a
dead news period just too tempting for her?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: I am not going to rise to that  particular bait and the barb,
because, frankly, it does not actually do the member justice. In fact, I think it is
important to consider the fact that I ha ve already answered the question—that I am
considering it. I am awaiting the advice to me from the Hon Rob Fisher QC, a former
High Court judge of New Zeala nd, and I expect to have it either today or tomorrow. I
expect that once I have it, I am  going to consider whether or  not to release both reports.
Because of the concerns that are out in the public, and, clearly, Mr Bain is concerned
and his supporters are concerned, I want to make sure that we have information that can
be relied on.

items.speaker: Charles Chauvel
items.text: Has Robert Fisher QC  received the same level of disclosure of
documents and other material afforded to  Justice Binnie by her predecessor, and, in
particular, will he be given access to any material produced by the Crown Law Office or
other officials that contains analysis that is critical of Justice Binnie’s report?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: I can advise the member that Mr Fisher, from memory,
has not been provided with any Crown Law a dvice. It is a matter that the Attorney-
General has not waived privilege on. I think it is important to note that Mr Fisher’s
advice to me will be a peer review of Justice Binnie’s report. It is not, in fact, under the
same terms of reference that Justice Binnie was provided with by my predecessor.

items.speaker: Charles Chauvel
items.text: In light of that answer, what we re the terms of reference given to
Mr Fisher QC, and how can the public have any confidence that the fruits of that
exercise will bear out the criticisms that sh e has made of Justice Binnie’s report, if he
has not seen those criticisms, a summary of them, or the advice leading to them?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Mr Speaker, could you ask the member to repeat his
question?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Certainly. Charles Chauvel, please.

items.speaker: Charles Chauvel
items.text: How can the public be confident, in light of her question, that the
result of Robert Fisher QC’s review of the report by Justice Binnie can be
comprehensive or satisfying, in light of the fact that he appears not to have any access to
the analysis that she clearly has had of criticism of the report?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: I think the Hon Justice Fisher’s advice to me will be
comprehensive, and I expect that the terms of reference that Justice Binnie was provided
7462 Questions for Oral Answer 12 Dec 2012
with by my predecessor either will be cont ained in that report or I will be happy to
provide them.
Health Services—Smoking Cessation, Immunisation, and Prescription Charges
6. Dr PAUL HUTCHISON (National—Hunua)  to the Minister of Health : What
progress has the Government made on its national preventive health targets this year?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Very good progress. Clinicians in the
district health boards and gene ral practice continue to provide more and more patients
with advice and support to quit smoking. Enga ging with a clinician is internationally
proven to be one of the most effective ways to quit smoking. Latest reports say there are
70,000 fewer New Zealanders smoking today than there were 3 years ago, and the rate
of daily smoking for youth has fallen dramatically from 14 percent in 2006-07 to 6
percent in 2011-12. This year’s child immunisa tion results show that  there is virtually
no difference in the rates between ethnicities or family income. Immunisation rates for
the richest families are the same as for the poorest families. As you know, immunisation
is one of the most effective interventions to prevent against infectious diseases in
children.

items.speaker: Dr Paul Hutchison
items.text: What further work is planned for preventative health in the new
year?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: There were over 4,000 notified cases of whooping cough this
year, of which 120 babies were hospitalised. Th is severe cough can cause babies to stop
breathing and can lead to blindness, brain damage, and, in severe cases, death. I am
pleased to announce to the House today th at the Government will announce this
afternoon that a free whooping cough vaccine, B oostrix, will be made available to all
pregnant women in New Zealand from 1 Janua ry next year until the current outbreak
finishes, to help protect their babies from th is potentially fatal disease. We are advised
that vaccinating mothers is the best way to provide ongoing protection for babies. On
top of this, the Government also encourages  parents to have their babies vaccinated
again at 6 weeks.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Is part of this dynamic progress being made under his
administration the circumstance where pharmacies  are being told that the Ministry of
Health will not be financing any signs aler ting people in New Zealand to the rise in
pharmaceutical costs on 1 January next year?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: That is not correct. There is going to be a flyer that will be
available in all pharmacies.
Whānau Ora, Minister—Confidence
7. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader—NZ First)  to the Prime Minister: Why
does he have confidence in the Minister for Whānau Ora?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Because she is a hard-working Minister
who is committed to improving outcomes for vulnerable families in New Zealand.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: How can he have confidence in a Minister who allowed the
Mongrel Mob to receive $20,000 of taxpayers’ money?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: My understanding is that, in te rms of that, the funding largely
came from another area, and on that basi s the belief was th at it would do good
improvement.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Does he share the Minister ’s view in respect of the
Mongrel Mob receiving $20,000 from the taxpayers  that “Had they utilised the funding
to pay wages to themselves, then there would have been no issue in terms of the use of
the money.”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: It would depend on how the money is applied and what that is
for. I mean, it is technically possible for peopl e in that situation to be applying it to a
programme, but it would depend on how it works.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Is he aware that on numerous  occasions this year—at least

of all Wh ānau Ora applicants who have received funding in the past year have been

items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Does the Prime Minister agree with the

Police Resourcing—Regional Distribution of Officers
8. KRIS FAAFOI (Labour—Mana) to the Minister of Police: Is she committed to
all of her promises in regards to the New Zealand Police?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: For which areas of New Zeal and has she delivered on the
Government’s 2008 election promise of ensuri ng a ratio of one pol ice officer to every
500 people?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Under this Government we have delivered an extra 600
police officers, who have been trained and are out working around New Zealand doing a
fantastic job.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker—[Interruption]
7464 Questions for Oral Answer 12 Dec 2012

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Let me just check. Is the honour able member quite finished?
[Interruption] Order! I can understand the point of order being raised because the
question actually asked in which regions ha s the undertaking of one police officer for
every 500 people—or something along those lin es—been achieved. The Minister gave
information, but she did not actually answer  that question. She may not have that
detailed information, which is not her fault.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: That was no promise of this Government. We promised, and
delivered, an extra 600 police across New Zealand.

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: I seek leave to table a document from the Parliamentary Library
showing that the ratio of sworn police to people for the South Island in 2012 was 1:573.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?
There is no objection.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: Is she or the police considering th e shifting of 200 to 300 constabulary
or non-constabulary positions fr om the South Island to the No rth Island in the next few
years; if so, what is being considered?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: That member well knows that the disposition of staff is an
operational issue. The Policing Act that wa s passed by the Labour Government made
that very clear. But what I can guarantee and I have promised as Minister of Police is
that there will be more front-line polici ng hours under this Government continually,
year on year, than there ever were under Labour.

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: Can she assure South Islanders th at between 200 and 300 constabulary
or non-constabulary positions will not be shifted from the South Island to the North
Island in coming years?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: That is not my undertaking to make. That is a decision made
by the commissioner on where those police would be best used in order to create safe
communities. Under this Government we ask for more front-line hours, that they stick
to their budget, and for a safe community.

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: Has she been briefed by the Commi ssioner of Police or police officials
about the shifting of 200 to 300 constabulary or non-co nstabulary positions from the
South Island to the North Island in coming years?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: No, and I would not expect to.

Better Public Services Targets—Justice Sector
9. TIM MACINDOE (National—Hamilton West)  to the Minister of Justice :
What progress has been made towards achie ving Better Public Services across the
justice sector?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Excellent progress has been made.
The crime rate is at the lowest level in 30 years, the justice sector has developed a range
of projects to further reduce crime and re offending, major steps have been taken to
improve support for victims of crime, a nd for the first time in two decades, the
Government has legislated to reduce the availability of alcohol by restricting rather than
relaxing the laws on the sale and supply of alcohol. I would like to thank those members
who voted for the Alcohol Reform Bill last night. Thank you very much. I appreciate it.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: What further results are expected?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: In the past year alone there have been more than 21,000
fewer crimes reported, with 3,000 fewer viol ent offences. That is thousands fewer
victims. For the first time in decades, the ju stice sector has an opportunity to focus on
12 Dec 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 7465
improving and streamlining its service delive ry. Our accessible just ice programme will
modernise our courts with the greater use of technology and better customer service.
Schools—Food Programmes
10. HONE HARAWIRA (Leader—Mana) to the Minister of Education: Does she
accept the finding of the Children’s Comm issioner’s Expert Advisory Group on
Solutions to Child Poverty that a government funded f ood programme in low-decile
schools is a simple, do-able, and low-cost soluti on to help children in poverty learn and
achieve at school, and the recommendation that Government design and implement
such a programme; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: No; because it is neither simple
nor low cost. The National Government is alre ady doing a lot in this area. We increased
the amount spent on hardship by almost 50 percent from 2008 to 2011. In 2011 we
spent $46 million on grants for food parcel s. KidsCan has received funding from the
Government. That has resulted in 4,500 children a day in 223 schools receiving food.
We provide a Fruit in Schools scheme, which is  available to all decile 1 and 2 primary
and intermediate schools, which results in about 97,000 students receiving a piece of
fruit each day, and we fund $174 million per annum through decile-based resourcing
policies.

items.speaker: Hone Harawira
items.text: How does the Minister respond to the comments in the latest report
of the Children’s Social Health Monitor  highlighting the fact that  tens of thousands of
children are being hospitalised for poverty-re lated illnesses, and does she agree that
addressing the root causes of poverty will help address the problem she has identified as
the one in five children not achieving their full potential at school?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: We know that the two best in vestments that can be made
within schools to raise achievement for five  out of five children are the quality of
teaching and the quality of leading, and, of course, other causes outside of school must
also be addressed, and that is why our Government is working on both.

items.speaker: Hone Harawira
items.text: How, then, does the Minister respond to the views of the 300
children consulted as part of the expert a dvisory group’s work who listed as their top
priority the issue of hunger and the importan ce of food in schools to  enabling kids to
focus and achieve at school, and the very strong support from the 1,800-plus individuals
and groups who gave feedback to the e xpert advisory group also recommending
Government-funded food in schools programmes?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I respond by saying that of c ourse it is a concern to our
Government, and that is why we are working hard in education to raise achievement.
That is why my colleague is working really hard in social development to support those
families that need support. That is why the rest of this Government is focused on how
we build a strong and resilient economy so th at we can have sustainable responses to
these issues.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Does she stand by the reason sh e gave for not supporting food in
schools that “The Government is playing its  part. In 2011 the Mi nistry of Social
Development spent $62 million on food parcels.”,  and does not this just prove the point
that many families simply do not have enough to get by, and are reliant on capped food
parcels to survive?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I stand by my statement that in 2011 $46 million was spent
on grants for food parcels, and in 2010 it wa s $60.2 million. I am advised that those are
the figures. The point it proves is that our Government is prepared to make additional
support available to those families that find it di fficult to meet these needs. So, yes, I do
stand by my comments.

Schools, Residential Special—Consultation and Judicial Decision on Proposed
Closures
11. CHRIS HIPKINS (Labour—Rimutaka)  to the Minister of Education : Does
she believe that her consultation process around the possible clos ure of residential
special schools provided all those affected with an opportunity to have a meaningful say
and have that say properly considered; if so, why?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Yes, I do; because the
opportunity was offered over several months. That response was given in the form of
surveys, reports, forums, hui, and fono. I took the opportunity to read all of the
submissions that were provided. It was the i ssues of the availability of coeducational
provision at Halswell Residential College and of sufficiency of safety that have resulted
in the High Court decision. I do not intend to appeal this decision. To provide certainty
for the current pupils and their parents at Salisbury School I can confirm that Salisbury
will remain open for 2013.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Did she ask for or receive any advi ce to contradict the research put
forward by the board of Salisbury School s howing that girls with intellectual
impairment are more vulnerable to sexual abus e in coeducational settings than they are
in a single-sex school; if not, why did she not ask for that information?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I did ask for advice from th e Ministry of Education and
received it. Moreover, the research that the member is referring to, which is a report by
Professor Briggs, was not submitted in full to me, nor was it submitted as part of the
consultation process. In fact, the High Cour t indicated that I could not have taken
account of it, because it was not submitted.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Why did the Ministry of Educa tion not provide her with that
research, which was available prior to her decision making, if she asked for all of the
relevant research and information on this issue?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I did ask for that advice, and I get the advice that is given
to me. Now I have asked for the ministry to  provide further advi ce on this important
issue, because, of course, safety is paramount in my considerations.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Why should the public have c onfidence that she executed her
decision-making responsibilities appropriate ly, given that Justice Dobson concluded
that it was “common sense” that the risk of sexual abuse for girls with impaired intellect
was likely to increase, that “No great leap in  logic is required to recognise the validity
of concerns …”, and that her argumen ts amounted to “an abrogation of the
responsibilities involved in making a decision”?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: In the first instance it is an existing requirement that no
residential home may take on placement in that residential home any child or young
person who has a previous sexual history. Seco ndly, I was assured by Halswell that it
was making professional and clin ical provision. Indeed, I think that in an emotional
issue as this is, it is very unfortunate that Halswell boys, their parents, and the
professional staff there are being impugned because it suits the defence.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The rules about bringing
High Court judges into disrepute, saying that  they are impugning people, and criticising
this court are quite strict. She is meant—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I did not interpret what th e Minister said as doing that. She
has not directly criticised a judge at all. The member is correct that she must not do that,
but I have listened carefully and I do not be lieve that the Minister  did that. A general
reference to the approach being taken he re as impugning the reputation of people
managing that institution I do not think can be interpreted as being a direct criticism of
the judge.
12 Dec 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 7467

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. The Minister’s comments can
be taken only as criticising the judge or as criticising me. If  that reference was directed
at me, I take offence at it. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Implied in the member’s questioning has been quite severe
criticism of the Minister, and for the Minister to—[Interruption] Order! For the Minister
to imply some criticism in her answer back I do not think is totally unreasonable. For
the member to believe that that is offensive to him—at the end of the day, if the member
has seriously taken offence, I obviously must ask the Minister to withdraw her
comment. But we have got to be careful. I ha ve sat here today listening to interjections
where I have heard members of this House accused of being liars, and it just troubles
me that members think that they can abuse e ach other across the House, and then get all
worked up over something that is far more mild. I just think we have got to be more
consistent and more reasonable in the wa y we respond to situa tions. If the member,
having reflected on it, has taken serious offence to it, then I have got to respect his view,
but I ask members just to be more reasona ble. As I say, I have  heard today members
accused across the House of being liars. I ha ve done nothing about it, because I do not
want to draw attention to these kinds of things. I just wish that members would be a
little more respectful. So I come back to th e member. If he has taken serious offence, I
will—supplementary question, Chris Hipkins.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Why did she ignore the advice of Peter Campbell, a trustee of
Salisbury School and chief executive of a residential facility for young people and
adults with intellectual disabilities, who advised her in a meeting on 16 October this
year that when that facility had operated as  a mixed-sex residentia l facility for a brief
period, the incidence of abuse increased markedly?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: In that very same meeting the Salisbury School board put
forward a proposal for its own provision of  coeducational schooling at Salisbury.
Moreover, we have 29 day special schools in New Zealand. They are all coeducational.
We have residential homes for those with disabilities that are run by a number of non-
governmental organisations, and they are coeducational.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Why should the public have any confidence in he r ability to
reconsider the matter, given that she was pres ented with clear eviden ce that the risk of
abuse, including sexual abuse, was likely to increase if she went ahead with the plan to
merge single-sex residential schools into a co educational facility, received no evidence
to contradict that claim, de spite asking for it, and yet we nt ahead with the decision
anyway?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Because I hold the providers of  residential schools in very
high regard. Halswell is sta ffed by professionals and clinic als, and had made it clear
what the provision would be: separate ac commodation, secure systems of security,
student advocates, full awareness of parents and their involvement and influence, the
availability of individual e ducation plans—all of these we re traversed and taken into
consideration. So I think that  I do show a commitment not only to excellent provision
but to how we might expand it to include even more young people into the system.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: How does she reconcile that statement that she has just made with
the statement of Justice Dobson that it wa s exactly that line of argument from the
Minister that he described as “an abrogation of the responsibilities involved in making a
decision”, and that she should not place all of  the responsibility for those matters on to
the school board of trustees?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: My regard for residential schools was supplemented by the
advice I received from the Ministry of Edu cation, which is responsible for the delivery
of special needs to children a ll around the country. This incl udes taking into account all
7468 Questions for Oral Answer 12 Dec 2012
of the submissions made by the parents, students, wh ānau, aiga, teachers, principals,
and clinicians.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Does she stand by the statement in her affidavit to the High Court
that “If for whatever reason it is no longer possible to close the school, effective from
27 January 2013, I am open to considering a differe nt effective date of  closure.”; if so,
what confidence can that community have that  she will reconsider her decision with an
open mind?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I do stand by that statement. In fact, as I answered in my
primary response, the board ha s already been advised that the school will remain open
for 2013, that I will meet with the board at the earliest possible opportunity in the new
year, and that we will together work through what the best outcome will be.
Welfare Reforms—Progress
12. MELISSA LEE (National)  to the Minister for Social Development : What
progress has the Government made in 2012 to shift the focus of our welfare system to
one that is active, work focused and delivers better outcomes for New Zealanders?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: There has been a
substantial year for those who are on welfar e, and we have been making a fundamental
difference for them. We are backing people in to work and we are seeing evidence of
that happening. Let me give you an example.  In the 4 years from November 2008 to
now, 305,000 people have left the benefit to star t work. This compares, of course, with
just 280,000 in the previous 4 years, under Labour. People are getting into work under
this Government.

items.speaker: Melissa Lee
items.text: How are the Government’s cha nges making a difference to those
receiving welfare? [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I apologise to the Minister. She has not even opened her
mouth yet and the level of interjection makes it impossible to hear. This is the last
question for the year and I just ask that we can hear the answer.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I understand their jealousy of  me, and that they just
cannot quite pull off animal prints, as I can. I have been getting a sense of that from
them today, but that is OK. I think what we  need to be proudest of is actually the
difference that we have made for young people. That, in fact , is a fact. What we have
seen is that youth on the unempl oyment benefit is 12 percent lower than this time last
year and 33 percent lower th an 2 years ago. Youth are gett ing the best go under this
Government. Happy 2012 and merry Christmas to the Opposition.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I move, That the House do now adjourn
until 2 p.m. on Tuesday, 29 January 2013 and that the sitting days in 2013 be as
follows:
January 29, 30, and 31;
December 3, 4, 5, 10, 11, and 12.
As the parliamentary year dr aws to an end can I take th is opportunity to offer my
best wishes for a very merry Christmas and a happy New Year to all members. Mr
Speaker, can I wish you the very best fo r your Christmas. I hear these endless
circulating rumours that this may be your last Christmas as Speaker of the House. If that
proves to be the case, then can  I not only wish you the very best for your time in other
roles but also say to the House that I believe that you will go down in history as one of
the greatest Speakers who has presided over th is Parliament in a fair and meaningful
way.
Can I take a moment on behalf of all MPs to thank the parliamentary staff who do so
much to help all of us, a nd that includes security, th e messengers, the Visits and
Ceremonial Office, IT, the Parliamentary Library, the Clerk’s Office, the select
committee staff, Hansard, all of the executive assistants who work for MPs, and our
electorate agents. Can I take a moment to  acknowledge Cabinet and, in particular, the
Deputy Prime Minister, Bill English, who has done, yet again, a fantastic job of
assisting us through. I say to the National Part y caucus that I wish you all the very best
for a very merry Christmas and a wonderful tim e back in your electorates. Of my office
staff I thank Wayne Eagleson, in particular , and Emma Holmes, w ho look after me so
well. I thank the staff in all the Ministers’ offices and the people who look after me
through the year, of course: th e drivers of the VIP Transpor t Service, the Diplomatic
Protection Squad, and, at my electorate offi ce, Mel and Genelle, who do such a great
job.
The year has ended where it started. The National Party caucus is united, focused,
and delivering a brighter future. That is in contrast to the Labour Party caucus, which,
once again, is divided, disillusioned, and pondering its futu re. In a way, Grant
Robertson summed it up best . He is 100 percent behind Da vid. Aren’t they all? The
question, though, is which David? That is the one we are worri ed about. That will, of
course, be the question that David Shearer will be pondering as he cuts his turkey on
Christmas Day. Does he have the numbers or is he in more trouble than Skippy in a
bushfire? That is roughly where he is going. David Shearer knows one thing: David
Cunliffe is not happy being just the MP fo r New Lynn. He is plotting, he is scheming,
he is ringing the unions, and he is havi ng barbeques all over the show, and, unlike
David Parker, he can count to 14. He knows the magic number, and there he is.
But I must say, as we go off to the parliamentary Christmas drinks tonight with the
press gallery, can you imagine what it would have been like at the Labour Party caucus
7470 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 12 Dec 2012
drinks? Goodness knows what happened when they started sending each other
Christmas cards. What on earth did David Sh earer write to David Cunliffe in his
Christmas card? “Thanks for all your hard work, DC, and support during the year. Your
loyalty means a lot to me.” Still, it could have been worse. Labour could still have Chris
Carter in its caucus, and the truth is that Parekura Horomia thinks he still is in the
caucus. Mind you, Parekura Horomia thinks He len Clark is leading the party, and most
of them wish she was, including David Shearer. In February we have a real treat coming
up, and that is the Labour Party equivalent of The X Factor. We know that one of them
is getting voted off, we just do not know which one.
But let us give credit where credit is due . Labour ended the year with one policy.
There was only the one policy, and the fact that  it did not add up or make sense is fair
enough. Labour’s policy was to build 100,000 homes for $300,000 each, mainly in
Auckland. Not to worry that David Parker  thinks it is 700,000 homes—that is OK.
There is a minor possible drawback, and that  is that the home does not come with a
section—as long as you are happy with that—or the section does not come with a home.
They will be clouds floating above Auck land. Those homeowners will walk off the
steps and they will think they are Felix Baumgartner. They will be falling 60,000 feet to
terra firma. There will not be anything there, but there you go.
Then there were the Greens. Well, the ha lf-whiff of a decent poll and there was
Russel Norman down at Working Style getti ng a new suit. You would think he would
be a bit reasonable. He wants to be the Mi nister of Finance. No wonder David Shearer
thinks it is a good idea. It is because David Parker cannot add up, and that is the basic
prerequisite for a Minister of Finance. It took me a year—I am prepared to accept that—
but I have finally worked out what green growth  is. It is this: printing $20 bills. That is
green growth under a Labour-Greens Govern ment. You can only imagine it, Russel
Norman as the Minister of Finance ringing Be llamy’s: “I will have a mung bean burger
with double alfalfa. Add in a bow l of fries and $5 billion a nd get it to my office by this
afternoon.”
Then there is New Zealand First. That pa rty ended the year with a lovely caucus
singalong. It went a bit like this: “Eight in the bed and Winston said ‘Roll over, roll
over.’ So they all rolled over and one fell out . There were seven in the bed and Winston
said ‘Who’s next?’.” That is the question—who is next? We really do not know. But my
advice is do not ring the TAB and do not go to the Wingatui races on Boxing Day.
Other than that you will be exactly fine. I will not start with the Mana Party, because let
us be honest, Hone did what he does best. He got arrested in 2012 and that was it.
In the worst of economic times this National Government continues to deliver for the
people of New Zealand. [Interruption] Labour does not want to hear it. Those members
want to pretend they live in a world where a ll these things have not  gone on, but let us
have a look. The deficit is half what it was last year, and we are on track to be in surplus
by 2013-14. There were 65,000 more jobs over th e last 3 years. Labour and the Greens
went out there—[Interruption] That is right. Apparently, there is a manufacturing crisis,
yet sales by volume are up 5.4 percent for the year to September. Homeowners across
New Zealand are paying the lowest interest rates for 50 years. Real wage growth is
taking place for New Zealande rs, and, yes, the real afte r-tax wage gap between New
Zealand and Australia has narrowed under our  watch. We have a 90-day probationary
period, which has allowed lots of New Z ealanders to get a job, and now a youth
starting-out wage will do the same. There are time limits for large consents on projects,
so that we can start seeing, as  we have, the likes of roads of national significance being
rolled out, just like in Te Araroa, where I wa s the other day. We have a new system for
processing oil and gas permits so  that we can take advantag e of those natural resources
in an environmentally friendly way that is fa ir. The roll-out of ultra-fast broadband has
12 Dec 2012 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 7471
begun across the country for New Zeala nders. Yesterday this Government
comprehensively won its court case for the mi xed-ownership model, and next year we
will see those shares going to the market. The negotiations for the Trans-Pacific
Partnership, a free-trade agreement worth US$3 billion a year to th is country, are well
and truly under way, as are the negot iations now for the ASEAN Regional
Comprehensive Economic Partnership a nd many other free-trade agreements—
something a Greens-Labour Government does not want a bar of. That is what is
happening economically.
The health system—you do not see it on th e front page every day. Why? Because
Tony Ryall is doing a magnificent job with th e health system in New Zealand. These
are not times where there are New Zealanders  consuming miles and miles of debt, and
on the back of that making their own bala nce sheets worse but pa ying the Government
of the day extra tax on this . These are tough and difficu lt times, and yet, under those
conditions, we have extended free doctors’ vi sits to under-6-year-olds right across the
country. We have rolled out rheumatic fever prevention programmes to 148 schools
across the country, helping 28,000 children, and by next year it will be 50,000 children.
Elective surgery—35,000 more operations a year  are taking place under this National
Government than when we inherited the place in 2008. For that tragic and terrible
disease that so many New Zealanders su ffer, cancer, the waiting times for cancer
treatment in this country have gone down considerably under a National-led
Government. There is a lot to be proud of in health.
Mr Speaker, you are giving me the message that it is time for me to sit down, so very
quickly let me just say the following: in welfare reform amazing reforms are taking
place under this Government, the crime rate  is down, hundreds of thousands of homes
are being insulated, and national standards are being bedded in and information is going
to parents.
Can I wish you all the very best for a merry  Christmas. To the National caucus I say
have a great time and see you in 2013. Be pr oud of what you have achieved. We have
ended where we started the year: beating those guys and leading New Zealand to a
brighter future.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: Can I—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I apologise to the Leader of the Opposition. Order! I ask that
courtesy be shown, please.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: Can I also start by wishi ng everybody here a very merry
Christmas and a happy New Y ear, and also by thanking you, Mr Speaker, for the way
that you have handled the goings -on in the House over the pa st year with dignity and
patience. I wish you all the ve ry best with your future, whenever that might be. We
know that whoever is going to fill your shoes, whether it be Maurice Williamson or Tau
Henare, will have big shoes to  fill—that is, when Steven  Joyce makes up his mind who
is going to be the Speaker. So thank you for your time in the Chair.
Thank you also to all of those people in  and around the Parliament who make this
place work: to the staff in our offices, who work the long hours working for our MPs
and supporting them; to the messengers, who keep the information flowing; to the
cleaners, who make our offices livable; to  the cafe workers, who keep us fed and
caffeinated; and to the security guards, who k eep a watchful eye on us all. I would also
like to thank the parliamentary staff in the Office of the Clerk for their work on research
and on legislation. All of thos e people do their job with  good humour, with patience,
and with grace, putting up with us politicians.
Thank you also to the other leaders of the O pposition parties. We are like a family in
many ways. We do not always agree, but usually we make it work, although, thankfully,
like some families, it is probably a good idea that we do not spend Christmas together.
7472 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 12 Dec 2012
Finally, thank you to the press gallery for wh at can be described only as fair and
balanced reporting of my firs t and honeymoon year. I love your work as much as you
say you love mine.
For the Government this is the year its members would like to forget, and many of
them have tried very hard to do exactly that. The year 2012 will be described as the year
of the brain fade—the year th at the PM’s memory suddenly went “Dot-gone”. It is the
year that has spawned a whole new lexicon of one-liners like, if you can recall, “I can’t
remember.”, “I don’t recall.”, “I haven’t read that report.”, “I don’t have that piece of
paper with me.”, and, my personal favourite, “That’s one person’s re collection.” I have
another movie idea for Warner Bros and it is called Partial Recall.
It started with John Banks and John Key havi ng that cup of tea together over a year
ago. Both could not remember the conversatio n. But it later turned out that they were
actually talking about New Zealand First an d senior citizens, including one senior
citizen whom they knew very well toge ther, Don Brash. John Banks continued the
theme. He did not remember meeting Dotcom , despite being flown to his mansion in a
helicopter for dinner and meeting Dotcom’s wife, whom he described as the most
beautiful woman in the world. I can tell you that  if I had said that to another woman in
the presence of my wife, she would never let me forget.
John Key caught that brain fade bug. He did not want to read about Banks, because
he would need to remember what he said  about ethical standa rds and to answer
questions. He did not recall he aring about the new resident of the largest mansion in
New Zealand—in his electorate. He did not recall that Kim Dotcom was wanted by the
highest levels of the US establishment. He did not recall knowing about the
Government Communications Security Bur eau, his own spy agency, listening to Kim
Dotcom’s conversations. He could not recall speaking to the bureau staff about it either.
He did not know that his Deputy Prime Minist er signed a once-in-a -decade ministerial
certificate to try to hush up that spying. The reality is not that he did not know. The
reality is that he did not want to know.
Yes, this Prime Minister has forgotten a lot this year, from how he voted on the
drinking age, whether he did a backroom deal  for more pokies with Skycity, to exactly
who it actually was who landed at the Welli ngton Airport just last week from the
intelligence agencies of the United States.
But I am sure that there is one thing that we can be quite clear about: he is unlikely to
receive a Christmas card from the Beckha ms this year. Remember too that David
Beckham spent years at Manche ster United wearing a gay red shirt every week. I recall
that it was after the comments that the Prime Minister made, about a week later, that he
was seen alongside other world leaders in  one of those pink, shiny numbers with
shoulder pads, strutting his stuff. And I thought: “Karma gets you in the end.”

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Carmen!

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: Or Carmen. The National Party might want to forget, but New
Zealanders, as they go into the barbecue and the Christmas season, will not forget. What
is it that this Government  would like you to forget? Well, unemployment is at the
highest level in 13 years. In fact, it is at  the highest level since National was last in
Government. Exports are down by 11 percent.  Inequality increased by the highest
amount in the OECD to the hi ghest level in our recorded history. The current account
deficit is the highest in the developed world, exceeding that of Greece. And, as one
member of our party likes to say, we have the worst economic growth in 50 years. Each
week 1,000 Kiwis are just giving up and going to  Australia. Why? Because they cannot
see an economic plan. Because the economic pl an that this Government has is basically
about selling stuff.
12 Dec 2012 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 7473
When you look at what is being sold, you realise not only that it is a bad idea, but
actually the price for what you are going to get is going to hit an all-time low, whether it
be Mighty River Power, Meridian Energy, So lid Energy, or Air New Zealand. But that
is OK because we can sell rural land! Our ag ricultural land can still be flogged off. Or
you can reach into the pockets of problem gamblers and subsidise Skycity—another
great economic idea. When you run out of al l those ideas, then comes the big idea,
which is about rebuildi ng Christchurch. When that is th e big idea that the Government
has for economic growth, then  you know there are no ideas th at this Government really
has for creating economic growth in this country.
Then it would like you to forget a number of  other things, the number of times that
sensitive data made it out into the public: ACC, the Ministry of Social Development, the
Inland Revenue Department, and I could keep on going. Then you come to education,
and this is what you would li ke to forget as well. E ducation—remember those class
sizes that were going to be increased to actually enhance teacher quality? Then there
were charter schools. You did not actually ha ve to be a qualified teacher in order to
teach in a charter school, to make that even  better. Then there is the idea to close down
the schools in Christchurch even if they do not need to be closed down. By the way, you
do not need to talk to anybody before you actually go out ther e and do it. It used to be
that when you criticised the education mini stry you still got paid  at the end of the
month. Not any more. No, there is no guarantee of that either.
So as we go into Christmas we reflect back on the year and we realise that it has been
a dismal one for New Zealand. But there is  an upside—there is an upside. And the
upside is that it has been a year of opport unity for the Opposition. So I would like to
give credit where credit is due, and thank the Government for the help it has been giving
to the Opposition all year, providing those easy targets, setting the bar to new even
lower levels, and achieving none of its goals and promises. It is a year that it would love
to forget, and some of it, it already has. I would like to encourage it to keep it up as we
go into the holiday season.
Finally, I would just like to say once again to everybody here, because I do not
believe people appreciate sometimes how  hard everybody works, a very merry
Christmas, a happy New Year, and please have  a restful and safe holiday. Thank you
very much.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Tēnā koe. Tēnā koutou katoa e te Whare.
Ngā mihi o te Kirihimete ki a koutou katoa.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Kia ora.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Kia ora.
Where will you go these holidays? Are you lucky enough to have a bach that is close
to the sea somewhere, a place that you and yo ur family have been going to now year
after year after year, for as far back as you can remember? Or maybe you have a
favourite motor camp to stay at—the kind of place where you have to muck in with
other families from all over the country, pitching your tents, peeling the spuds, herding
the tribes of children, and all done to the soundtrack  of the cricket th at is playing on
your neighbour’s radio.
The Kiwi summer holidays are something pr etty special, especially when you are a
kid. You can escape those pesky grown-ups a nd go on an adventure, often with a brand
new, day-old bestest friend ever. Those long, hot summer days seem to stretch on for
ever and ever until you can hardly keep your eyes open, and then before you know it
you are asleep to the sound of the moreporks calling. But then the new day breaks, cool
and full of potential, and you get another chance to master your skateboard or go fishing
for kai moana with your nanny and your koro a nd your cousins, or you are being asked,
yet again, to go and search for that extra c up of flour to help your mother, who has run
7474 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 12 Dec 2012
out for making her cake that day. These are the kinds of moments that we live for and
work hard to provide for our children and the children of our friends and our
neighbours. This is what Christmas is for ma ny of us, and this is what makes us truly
rich as New Zealanders.
But this is not the Christmas story fo r an increasing number of New Zealand’s
children, and it was not mine. I had a lot of freedom as a child in the summer holidays,
but we did not get to go away. Most of my holidays were spent wandering around those
dry, grassy paddocks of Ashhurst , dodging the thistles in our bare feet , trying not to get
electrocuted by the farmer’s fences, and waiting for our dad to come home from a day at
work so he could take us all down to the river for a swim.
Those were some of the best times of my summer holidays. We would mob our dad
when he drove up the driveway. Then there was the ride down to the river on the back
of his Holden Kingswood—can you remember  those—with the door down and our legs
hanging off the edge so that we could jump off and be the first to race to the cold, cold
water. My cousins and I, and my friends, and anyone else who was around would join in
to spend our evenings there doing dive-bom bs off the bank of the river, hunting for
bullies and for freshwater crays, and squealing about the eels that might come out and
bite us on the bum, and all under the watchful  eye of our dad, who was usually having a
good wash after a hard day’s work at the bread factory.
Our swimming hole at the Pohangina River was our place to forget about everything.
Down there it did not matter whether you were rich or poor, Māori or Pākehā, a boy or a
girl. The river brought us all together, and it gave us some of the happiest moments of
our childhood. We did not have  much, but I did have a wh ānau who loved and nurtured
me in a country that made sure that I had enough to eat, a good school to go to, and a
safe, clean river that I could spend my summer holidays swimming in.
That is a country to love. Th at is a country to fight for— a country that protects its
vulnerable, loves its beautiful environment, and empowers all of its children, rich or
poor, M āori or P ākehā, boy or girl, to become the best that they can be. That is a
country I want my kids and grandkids to grow  up in, and I want my neighbours’ kids to
grow up in it too, no ma tter who they are. I be lieve that this is a vision that we can
achieve only if we work together. I believe that this is actually the only way to live with
dignity and grace in this country. I believe that  this is what we, as  New Zealanders, in
our modest ways quietly yearn for.
But our lucky country is s lipping away from us from  right under our feet. Our
country has never been wealthier, yet the swimming hole of my childhood is now at risk
of being too polluted and unsafe to swim in, just like more than half of our lowland
rivers that are already so polluted. Our count ry has never been w ealthier, but we are
living at a time when the differences between us have never been wider. We are rapidly
becoming one of the most unequal countries  in the developed world, where once we
were one of the most equal.
Our country has never been w ealthier, but it is hard to remember a time when it was
so difficult to find an ordinary job that  paid a decent wage—enough to save up some
money and to be able to afford to take the kids away on holiday this Christmas. It is like
we have forgotten what it is like to sta nd alongside one anothe r and remind ourselves
that we are each our sister’s and our brother’ s keeper. But it does not have to be this
way if we choose to live with compassion and generosity—in the spirit of Christmas, no
less.
In this spirit, the Greens will continue to  work with others across this House to
realise our inclusive vision for our beautiful and abundant  country. With the National
Government we have delivered what is turni ng out to be the smartest investment in our
infrastructure that a Government could make: spending $340 million to insulate 240,000
12 Dec 2012 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 7475
homes, creating 2,000 jobs, sa ving the country money, savi ng lives, and keeping us
warm and dry.
It is good to be able to work across the political spectrum with the National Party and
with the Labour Party to deliver for our Ne w Zealand families. With the Labour Party
we have worked together on a citizens init iated referendum that will give the public a
vote on the sale of State assets. These are the assets that were built by our grandparents
for our grandchildren. With Labour, New Zeal and First, and the Mana Party we are
working together to protect the manufacturi ng jobs that remain—few as they may be—
and to find new tools to support more.
In this spirit of working together I want to finish by thanking all of those who enable
us to do our work here in the Parliament th rough their dedicated service. I am thinking
now of all the party staff that we each have in our offices, the Office of the Clerk, the
Select Committee Office, parliamentary secur ity, the cleaners, the caterers, the travel
office, the call centre, the library staff, a nd the Chamber and gallery officials who are
here with us today. You all make this place work. You go largely unnoticed by us MPs
and certainly by the public, bu t without you this democratic institution can simply not
function. I know it has not been  an easy time for you over this last 12 months, facing
cutbacks and redundancies, so please know th at the Green Party st ands in solidarity
with you. To you, Mr Speaker, thank you for your assistance and for your many years of
service to this Parliament.
May you all have a Christmas where your be llies feel full and your hearts feel
content. May you have a Christmas that is alive with hope and rich in compassion. May
you share the many gifts given to you this ho liday season, knowing that we can live
very well together in this spirit, helping others so that we may all live with dignity and
grace here in our beautiful country, Aotearoa New Zealand. Ngā mihi o te Tau Hou ki a
koutou katoa. Tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou katoa.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: It is a great pity that “Ronald
McDonald” is no longer in the House, because he could have learnt something from this
speech—

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: I raise a point of orde r, Mr Speaker. I thought it was a tradition of
this House that the absence of a member should not be referred to by another member.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Well, that is a valid point, but no member of the House
was named, which brings me to another poin t, that we should address members by their
appropriate name. Let us all just take a deep  breath, and the Rt Hon Winston Peters will
start again.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: It is a great pity that since she has been here Maggie
Barry has learnt absolutely nothi ng at all. The easiest way to catch her out is just to say
something, and, like a wanton shark come to  summer beaches, out goes her tongue and,
bang, that is it. She bites it every time.
On behalf of New Zeala nd First we want to tha nk all of the people whose
commitment, integrity, and professionalism ensu re that Parliament runs in a smooth
way: everyone in the Speaker’s office, the Clerk’s Office, the Hansard reporters, all the
library staff, and the telephonists. I acknowle dge especially all the messengers and their
cheerful manner around this precinct. We tha nk also the security guards for their hard
work in keeping us all safe, and the clean ers, who deserve a sp ecial thanks—and a pay
rise. They, like so many others, are not ge tting a fair go. Imagine how difficult it is to
clean up after these people. It cannot be an easy job. They deserve a much better pay
round and remuneration than they are get ting. If we have forgotten anybody, our
apologies.
We appreciate all who enable us to operate as an effec tive political party, and an
effective political party we ar e. The support and dedication of our staff have made this
7476 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 12 Dec 2012
year for New Zealand First a successful one. We have been effective. We have been
firm in opposition. We have been constructiv e. We have tried to help those in need,
such as the elderly and the young, and even farmers, who are being robbed blind by the
banks with swaps deals in this country—

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: What about grandma’s money?

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: —and all manner of people, in particular. And our
grandchildren—that is true. We have oppos ed the massive cuts in all sorts of
departments made for no sound reason and, worst of all, the disastrous treatment of our
No. 1 agency abroad, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade. It has been a disgrace,
an abysmal disgrace—hundreds of millions of  dollars lost. Our representation overseas
is second rate nowadays. We have become an international joke, and the Government
wants to say that it is doing something for this country!

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: You’re losing it. You’re losing it.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: I know why Mr Banks is laughing. It is because he
has never been held to account. This is th e man, who is laughing over there, who told
Parliament and told the country that the pol ice’s secret report was secret because the
police requested that. That is demonstrably and palpably not true. Mr Banks, is it or is it
not true that you requested the secrecy?

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
