items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. I hear the honourable
member saying “you this”, “you that”, and “ you did this”. I do not know what you have
done, Mr Deputy Speaker, but I am sure you have not done what he says you have done.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Technically, the member is correct, and that point of
order is upheld. Members should be just a little more careful about pronouns.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Mr Banks, this is the question: did Mr Banks request
that the police report be secret? Yes or no? [Interruption] I cannot hear him. Yes or no?

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: Where’s the money? Where’s grandma’s money?

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Yes or no? When we had a question about grandma’s
money—unlike his leader and unl ike him—we dealt to it. We  dealt to it. We did not
stand around making accusations. Remember, Mr  Horan’s mother made the allegations
in the codicil; we did not make them. We act ed. And here is Mr Banks, who forgot 42
cheques and a man who is unforgettable, a ma n whose place he went to on a helicopter,
whose wife he said was the mo st beautiful woman he had ever  met, and then he said he
did not remember him. Mr Banks, was it Mr  Banks who requested the police secrecy?
Yes or no?

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: What about natural justice?

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Yes or no? Look, the last thing Mr Horan needs is
natural justice. I tell you, when he gets it—[ Interruption] No, no, hold your tongue.
Hold your tongue, lad. Do not ge t carried away. When he gets it, he will fi nd that it is
the last thing he wants. We are totally conf ident of our actions. Is Mr Key confident of
his? No. He does not want to see the report. He does not even want to ask Mr Banks a
question. He does not even want to examine what he has been saying. Mr Banks, as a
Minister, what was told to the Prime Minister by the leader of the ACT Party was not
true, was it?

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: Grandma got run over by a reindeer.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Oh, there you are. There you are. He will not answer
the question. Look, I would have thought, even  at Christmas-time, the member could be
more overt, more open. No, no, no, he hides behind parliamentary secrecy and a useless,
incompetent, and non-transparent leader, “Mr Spray and Walk Away”.
The other thing we did this year was to get up a Reserve Bank bill that almost got
passed, and we thank those parties that helped  us. It would have helped New Zealand,
not the paper-shuffling speculators that Mr  Banks and others in the National Party
12 Dec 2012 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 7477
love—you know, the internationalists sitting over there in New York, playing against
our currency at 35:1. We would have st opped those people, but, no, no, the men who
call themselves the nationa lists in the National Pa rty—no, no—would rather be
globalists and forget their pe ople. The wonderful news, I mu st say, is that every day
now we are getting phone calls and letters from former National Party people who have
had a gutsful of them.

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: Name one.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: I could name hundreds—I could name hundreds. We
are getting all sorts of calls, because they know that the sell-out has been going on for
far too long.
I want to make something very clear to our  supporters out there, to whom we wish a
very happy Christmas, as well. To every New Zealand First supporter and worker and to
all those legion who are thinking of joining us , let me say this: the next election is not
going to be in 2014. It is coming much sooner than that. So have a good holiday, have a
good Christmas, but before the one after this Christmas, there will  be an election. Mr
Banks cannot hang on now. He cannot hang on the moment he gets exposed in court—
goodnight nurse. Goodnight nurse. There goes the ACT Party—no replacements, no
replacements.
I want to say that we also were lucky last week. We drew two bills from the ballot
that symbolise our ideals and policies. One will help children; the other will target
criminals who commit crime in the presence of a child.
So what has happened with the economy? Emigration from New Zealand is our
shame. Immigration into New Zealand is a shambles. Unemployment is rising. The
economy is reeling and staggering. Indebtedness is soaring. Incompetence and bungling
is that Government’s abys mal record—Dotcom and Banks, scandal after scandal after
scandal—and very soon it will be goodnight nurse, and not too soon.
What is those members’ greatest pride at  the end of the year ? They are going to
get—if the court does not stop th em—to sell the country’s herita ge. It is the asset sales.
“Mr Spray and, giggling like a schoolgirl , Walk Away”—Mr Key, giggling like a
schoolgirl—thinks that that is a great accomplishment. “We’re going to sell the
birthright.”, he said.
Anyway, let me just say this here. This is where he should give in, because the
National Party used to always go on about th e nanny State, but this is how bad things
are. I have heard there are dreadful reports coming into my office about the treatment of
Santa Claus, also known as Father Christmas,  at North City Plaza in Porirua. On the
evening of 5 December, it was noticed that Mr Claus, or Santa as we know him, was
thin and the cheeks of his face were pale. Mr Claus revealed to my office that the health
authorities warned that they would no longer tolerate employing a Santa Claus who was
obese with high blood pressure . He has been forced to st arve himself for months and
take medication for high blood pressure, and he can hardly, barely, go “Ho, ho!”, let
alone “Ho, ho, ho!”. That is the kind of stat e that these little—I cannot say the word, of
course, but they were in Germany in 1935. That is the kind of country we have come to,
and there is worse to come.
It has been revealed that the “Ministry of Sexual Equality” has warned it will no
longer tolerate sexual stereotyping of the spirit of Christmas. That is right. Santa Claus,
as the case may be, is now going to be calle d “Person Christmas” as from next year.
Throughout history Sinterklaas, as he is known in his native North Pole, has been a
jolly, fat man with red cheeks. Now he is skinny, miserable, and pale.
New Zealand First is the party of traditiona l values. We stand firmly alongside Santa
Claus and his inherent right to be a jolly, fat man with red cheeks. We remind the health
police that Santa has been ar ound a lot longer than  they have, despit e his obesity and
7478 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 12 Dec 2012
high blood pressure. New Zealand First’s MP s will be hanging up their stockings as
usual. We will be leaving out food and drink fo r Mr Christmas, and it will be high in
sugar and saturated fat, and there will be a Christmas cake and port wine. We wish
every member in the House and their familie s a safe and enjoyable Christmas and—just
to make sure Mr Banks does not leave this Parliament as confused as ever—able to
write their own speeches, unlike him.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: T ēnā koe. Kia ora t ātau
katoa i tēnei ahiahi i a t ātau e mihi nei i t ētahi ki t ētahi, tātau ki a t ātau. Kua tū ake hai
waha k ōrero m ō te P āti M āori ki te tuku i ng ā mihi an ō hoki. Tuatahi ki te Rt Hon
Lockwood Smith, ahakoa k āre ia i te noho ki t ērā Tūru, ka mihi r ā, ka whai haere i te
āhuatanga o ngā kōrero ki a ia, me tāna whakahaere i te āhuatanga o te Whare Pāremata.
I tēnei wā ko te nuinga o ngā tāngata i roto i te Whare Pāremata, e mihi nei ki tēnā, ki
tēnā, kei te k ī atu: “Goodwill to all me n and women.” Koinei t ētahi kōrero ka puta i te
waha o w ētahi. Ia r ā, ia r ā ka haramai t ātau ki roto i t ēnei Whare P āremata me te
whakarongo ki te karakia e mea ana, kia ng ākaunui te tangata, t ētahi ki tētahi. Kia kaua
tētahi e whiu i te kupu a t ētahi ki t ētahi, “nek minnit”, ko taua āhua anō rā. Kua whiu i
aua k ōrero an ō hoki i t ētahi, p ēnā i t ērā tangata e amuamu n ā i te taha i a t ātau e
whakarite nei i te huarahi ki te Kirihimete.
Ko tā mātau ko te k ī atu, me hoki ng ā mahara ki te hunga kua ngaro i te tirohanga
kanohi, ko rātau e mihia ana i runga i ō tātau marae, i a au e tū nei, pēnei i te āhuatanga i
runga i ō tātau marae, ka hoki ng ā mahara ki te hunga kua ngaro. Ko Jacqui Te Kani
tētahi, ko Jean Puketapu t ētahi, ko Timi te Heuheu, ko Maruhaeremuri Stirling, ko
Wally Papa, ko Kateia Burrows, ko R ēnā Savage, ko Doreen McCorkindale, ko T ākuta
Hone Kaa tonu, ko T ākuta Joe Pere, Rev. Rau Kapa, ko M āmā Tere. Tae atu ki t ērā o
ngā mate in ā tatanei ki a Cassidy Tangaere, a R āwiri Te Whare, a T ākuta Arnold
Wilson, a Rata Pue, a John Nyman, a T ā Pita Tapsell. Ar ā noa atu w ētahi, nō reira, ka
huri ki te reo Pākehā mō te wā poto nei i tēnei wā.
[Thank you. Greetings to us all as we wish each other well individually and
collectively this afternoon. I ri se to speak on behalf of the M āori Party and to express
complimentary remarks as well. Firstly to  the Rt Hon Lockwood Smith, even though he
is not in that Chair, I commend him and follow on in the tenor of the accolades
expressed about how well he has conducted the business of Parliament.
At this moment, the majority in the House who are wishing this one and that one well
are actually saying: “Goodwill to all men and women.” This is a statement that will
emerge from the mouth of some. Each day we come into this House and listen to the
prayer saying that people should treat each  other kindly, then, “nek minnit”, it is back
to that situation all over again. Those disparaging remarks are tossed around once
again at one, like that person complaining over  there as we give due consideration to
the approach of Christmas.
We say to take the minds back to the ones who are no longe r seen, to those ones who
were acknowledged on our courtyards. I stand here before you, in very much a similar
manner as one does on our courtyards. And as I stand here memories go back to the
ones who have gone. Jacqui Te Kani is one , Jean Puketapu is another. Timi te Heuheu,
Maruhaeremuri Stirling, Wally Papa, Ka teia Burrows, Rena Savage, Doreen
McCorkindale, Dr Hone Kaa, Dr  Joe Pere, Rev. Rau Kapa, M āmā Tere, and Cassidy
Tangaere, who passed away just recently. R āwiri Te Whare, Arnold Wilson, R ātā Pue,
John Nyman, and Sir Peter Tapsell. There are m any others, and so I will turn to speak
in English now at this point for a short time.]
We have farewelled a number of those people, and I have mentioned their names, but
this complex has also had its share of trag edies and losses. We think of Anne Roberts
and Dave Allanson and other staff w ho are no longer with  us. Me waiho r ātau kia moe,
12 Dec 2012 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 7479
kia okioki. Ko r ātau tētahi rārangi tokoiti nei o te hunga kua ngaro, me whai whakaaro
tātau i a tātau e mihi nei, tātau ki a tātau.
Arā anō te kōrero mō tētahi kaupapa hōu kua whakaarahia ake e te Pāti Māori ko tērā
e pā ana ki te new normal. He aha t ēnei mea ko te new normal? Me k ī e ai ki tā wētahi,
ko Mitt Romney t ētahi i rongo nei i te ngau o te new normal. Ko te new normal ko t ērā
e kōrerohia ana ko te tuku i te rerek ētanga o te tangata ki te ao, ar ā ko te unleashing the
power of diversity. Ko te āhuatanga o t ēnei kaupapa ko te nohotahi o te t āne me te
wahine, o te nohotahi o te tamaiti me te pakeke, o te whakaaro ake o ng ā tamariki, ā, e
tika ana kia noho au i waenganui i t ētahi kāhui o t ērā iwi o t ērā takiwā o te motu, kia
taea ai te k ī, kai te tika t ērā momo noho. Ā-wairua, ā-karakia, ā-hāhi, he aha r ānei. He
mea pai kia tau te noho ki roto i tēnei huihuinga. Ko te āhuatanga o te economic growth,
me te economic justice, ēnei āhuatanga katoa. Engari, ko te mea nui o t ēnei mea o te
new normal, kia kaua t ātau e mataku ki t ēnei mea o te mataku. Me k ī, me titiro ki te
paerangi, ki mua i te aroaro.
Ko tā mātau ko te k ī atu, he wā tōna ka whakah ōnoretia te Tiriti o Waitangi. He w ā
tōna ka noho tonu t ātau i raro i te marumaru o t ēnei mea o te whanaungatanga, o te
honotahi a t ētahi ki t ētahi. Ar ā, ahakoa ko te rerek ē o te noho a t ēnā a t ēnā. Kia
whakatinanahia ēnei k ōrero katoa e k ōrerohia ana, ko te whanaungatanga, ko te
kotahitanga, ko te kaitiakitanga. Kia kaua e k ōrero engari me whakatinana i ērā kōrero.
Nō reira, ko tētahi kaupapa kua whakahaerehia e m ātau i tēnei tau ko tērā e pā ana ki te
Whānau Ora. Ka mutu, ko te tikanga o tērā he whakamana i ngā whānau kia kitea mai ai
i tētahi huarahi hei whāinga mō rātau ake. Kia kaua e waiho m ā te Kāwanatanga rātau e
aki, e pei atu ki tētahi huarahi kāre i te tino pīrangitia e rātau. Nō reira, kua eke.
[Allow them to rest and sleep. They are a sm all list of the ones who are gone, and so
we must pay our respects to them.
That aside, there is a new initiative that the Māori Party has raised that relates to the
new normal. So what is the new normal? Acco rding to some, Mitt Romney was hurt by
the new normal. The new normal is about unleash ing the power of diversity. It is about
a diverse range of people livi ng together in harmony. It includes economic growth and
economic justice. However, the main feature of  the new normal is that we must not fear
it for what it is. We need to focus on the distant horizon in front of us.
In time, the Treaty of Waitangi will be honour ed. In time, we will all live in harmony
despite our differences. Positive relationships, unity, and guar dianship will be realised.
We must walk the talk. One of the pr ogrammes we have managed this year is Wh ānau
Ora, which is about empowering wh ānau to find their own solutions, not just the
Government providing them with pathways that  do not really suit them. And so, it has
made it.]
Whānau Ora, as I have been saying, is obviously a key focus that we have had
plenty of interest in as a key, essential platform of the M āori Party. We have got to
some 34 provider collectives, with over 180 pr oviders involved, directly impacting on
33,000 New Zealanders who are fo cused on a better future. Wh ānau Ora facilitates
transformation within wh ānau, helping them to move fr om a state of dependency to
independence and, finally, interdependency. It is all about the deve lopment of solutions
by whānau themselves.
In this House we have had one politician who has been hell-bent on creating a myth
around Whānau Ora, but actually the reality is vas tly different. It was great to see the
Expert Advisory Group on Solutions to Child Poverty confirm support for the
continuation and expansion of the Wh ānau Ora approach to empower families and
children to identify goals and progress towards them. Its analysis also indicates that the
learning from this way of working could be applied across the Government and the
community to reduce child poverty and mitigate its effects.
7480 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 12 Dec 2012
At the same time as Wh ānau Ora has been gathering and garnering support, so too
have we seen the rise of M āori economic development. The launch this month of Hei
Kai Kei Aku Ringa—The Crown-M āori Economic Growth  Partnership had
unprecedented support from across business. The Māori Asset Base  report identified a
$36.9 billion M āori economy, and the strategy wo rks on the basis that the
entrepreneurship and innovation of the M āori economy is not only good for tangata
whenua but also good for the nation.
We recognise the huge progres s that has been made in Treaty settlements, and the
Māori Party has been pretty honoured to be ta king a role in thos e across the length and
breadth of the country. We refer specifically to ones like Ngāti Whātua o Kaipara, Ngāti
Whātua ki Ōrākei, Ng āti Manuhiri, Ng āti M ākino, Ng āti Manuhiri, Rongowhakaata,
and Waitaha to name a few, and there are more coming. What we do know is that every
one of the whānau, hapū, and iwi have a marae at their very hearts, and our commitment
to marae has been such that we have been  working to test an idea called Marae CBD,
using marae as hubs for education and employment opportunities for local communities.
One of the pieces of legislation that has made a particular impact in my rohe this year
has been that of the Mokomoko (Restoration of Character, Mana, and Reputation) Bill.
It certainly reinforces the view that we have as a party of knowing our histories and
knowing about ourselves. This is the basis behind our push for cultural competency in
the health and education sectors, and we have been pretty proud to see the progress
made by Tātaiako, which is having an impact in school s. It is bringing about the best in
ourselves in the education sector.
Unfortunately, far too many of our childr en have suffered over the years through
rampant neglect, the savage effects of  poverty, the compounding disadvantage of
institutional racism, and restri cted access to services. The M āori Party has absolutely
dedicated itself to the ta sk of supporting every wh ānau to be the best that they can, and
we have attempted to do this throughout the year. We have fought for the $24 million to
confront rheumatic fever—a Third World di sease that has no pl ace in Aotearoa. We
have consistently tackled through the tobacco reform a killer disease that takes the lives
of 5,000 New Zealanders every year. We have negotiated for 20,000 low-income homes
to benefit from home insulation, and we ha ve made great progress across a number of
areas. But there is still much to do. Our eyes are always on the state and health of the
future of our mokopuna and what they wi ll do into the future, so things like
environmental kura are important, as well.
As we wrap up I want to absolutely acknowledge and endorse the other comments of
support for the team within the parliamentar y precincts: the Office of the Clerk, Mary
Harris, the Deputy Clerk, the Ta ble Office, the library team , Hansard, of course, the
interpreters, the security team—the fantastic security team—the fantastic cleaning staff,
the staff of Copperfields and Be llamy’s, the IT team, which ha s really come to the fore
this year in giving us support, the buildi ngs and finance staff, the messengers, the
telephonists, the Parliamentary Service staff, and, of course, our own M āori Party team.
We miss some of the personali ties of the place, of course —those who have left this
year, including Beverley, and the likes of Clarrie, Raymond, Justin, Shirley, and Ernie.
Each of them and many more have done so mu ch to make this such a fine establishment
and to preserve the protocols to support the MPs and, most of  all, to do their best for
Aotearoa.
Of course, in closing, across the House we  want to acknowledge everyone’s views,
diverse as they might be, and our passion and determination to contribute to the well-
being of the nation. Although we may not necessarily agree with each other’s stance, the
general view that I would accept is that we ar e here for the best interests of Aotearoa—
including those who hold ministerial portfo lios and, indeed, select committee inquiries.
12 Dec 2012 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 7481
We thank everyone who has formed a part of this Whare. We wish everyone all the very
best, a wh ānau-focused Christmas, time to relax, to be with loved ones, to revitalise all
of ourselves, and to have a very merry Christmas. Ka kite ā te Tau Hōu. Ngā mihi nui o
te tau.
[See you in the New Year. Huge greetings of the year.]

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Just before I call the next speaker, I have quite a complex
arrangement of split calls and in order to tr y to keep this as seamless as possible I will
just call the member and give them their time—it will be either 5 or 10 minutes. If the
whips want to liaise with me they can do that , but I think that is the easiest way to go.
The next call goes to Hone Harawira—5 minutes.

items.speaker: HONE HARAWIRA
items.text: Tēnā koe. Tēnā koutou katoa e te Whare. I
know that this is a time when MPs traditionally say nice things about one another and
wish peace upon the world, but 2012 has been a nightmare for a growing population of
desperately poor people in this  country who have little to  celebrate. So I want to
dedicate my last words this year to highligh ting the plight that they face, to challenging
a Government that doles out favours to the rich while destroying the futures of those
with little future and fewer prospects, and to posing alternatives that we might all live
with.
This Government’s commitment to the free market has not just allowed but actively
encouraged businesses like Ports of Auck land and AFFCO to attack unions, reduce
safety standards, and cut wages in their ruth less drive for even greater profit margins.
Unemployment has continued to rise. M āori and Pasifika rates continue to be three
times higher than those for P ākehā. More and more people are being forced on to
benefits as they struggle to  cope, and the Government’s re sponse has been to cut youth
benefits, cut assistance to young mums, cu t unemployment benefits, cut off ACC to
those with genuine injuries, cut back on assistance to those needing a house, cut back on
State housing in communities like Glenn Innes,  arrest people for daring to hold those
communities together, evict families fr om State houses in communities like Ōtāngarei,
force people already living on the margins in to ever greater le vels of poverty and
desperation, and bully beneficiaries into jumping through hoops designed to shame and
humiliate them. Then Government members make smart alec remarks in this House and
snigger about their wittiness, as if  poverty and hunger and homelessness and
desperation and despair and suicide were thi ngs to celebrate, rather than problems to
alleviate.
Yes, things may be tough, but clearly not for everyone. The rich are getting richer,
the poor are getting poorer, and working people and those who cannot find work have
responded by simply upping sticks and leavi ng this country for a new life in Australia.
The real scary thing about that is that this  Government is showing by its policies that it
simply does not care enough about the future of  its own citizens to take steps to reduce
poverty, to create employment, to build homes  for its people, or to provide a positive
educational environment for our children.
In the face of massive public opposition, as shown by the 300,000-signature national
petition and a legal challenge to st op the sale of State assets until M āori interests in
water have been settled, this Government remains committed to the sale of New
Zealand - owned power companies. In the face of Petrobras’ forced withdrawal from an
unsafe and untested deep-sea oil drilling programme off the coast of Wh ānau-a-Apanui,
this Government not only remains committed to its strategy of exploiting fossil fuels but
also has opened up the Reinga Basin off Northland’s coast for more oil and gas
exploration programmes, regardless of the disastrous safety records of potential bidders.
In the face of overwhelming evidence from  the Children’s Commissioner’s Expert
Advisory Group on Solutions to Child Pove rty, the 2012 Children’s Social Health
7482 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 12 Dec 2012
Monitor, the Child Poverty Action Group, uni ons, teachers associations, and health
providers about the disa strous impact of this Government ’s policies on the children of
the poor, the Government refuses to accept that a comprehensive food in schools
programme will reduce the im pact of poverty and improve  educational outcomes for
children in low-decile schools. Instead it offe rs up a pointless tax credit regime that is
destined to fail because poor people have no awareness of how such arrangements work,
and will not apply for them if it means ha ving to go through the humiliation they are
subjected to every time they have to go into a Government agency.
That is why I am hugely proud of the effort s of members of the Mana movement all
around the country, and grateful to them for their commitment to change, their
willingness to lay their bodies on the line, and their steadfastness in the face of a cold-
hearted Government. I am proud that Mana me mbers have been on th e front line in the
battle to stop State asset sales, to support the New Zealand M āori Council bid to protect
Māori interests in water, to help keep our seas free of dangerous deep-sea oil drilling
programmes, to stand against the take over of New Zealand’s sovereignty by
multinational corporates, to stand alongside those fighting to keep their homes, to
support workers’ demands for safe working conditions and a decent living wage, and, of
course, to promote the notion that feeding kids  in schools is not an issue of cost but one
of justice.
So, as we come to the end of the year, let me just say thank you to everyone who
helps us around Parliament, and to all of  my parliamentary colleagues a simple
message: enjoy your break, enjoy your wh ānau, share your good fortune, a Mana
Kirihimete to you all, and a simple request  for 2013 that we all commit ourselves to
ensuring that every child in Aotearoa ge ts at least one decent meal every day. T ēnā
koutou, kia ora tātou katoa.

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BANKS
items.text: The hundreds of thousands of New
Zealanders who tune in to their crystal sets every afternoon at  2 o’clock, and the
hundreds of thousands of New Zealanders who watch Parliament on the telly every
afternoon and are riveted, will be saying to themselves today thank God that John Key,
the ACT Party, and the coaliti on are on this side of the H ouse, and the coalition of
losers is on that side of the House.
I want to thank David C unliffe. I want to thank the Opposition leader, David
Cunliffe—or is it David Shearer? On behalf of David Shearer I thank David Cunliffe for
all of the publicity that he has had in the la st 3 months, because it is more than he has
had in his total time as leader of the hapless Opposition.
Also this afternoon we heard from the pa rty that used to be known as “Winston
First”, now known as “TAB First”. I want to sa y thank you to the ageing leader of that
party for making me feel so good every day.  When I look at him, I understand how
important it is to look after yourself for 65 years.
To the Green Party, the party that want s to print money, to the old dudes and young
fogies of the Green Party, al l I can say when I look at th e leader of the Green Party
every day is that I simply cannot understand why Australia is richer than New Zealand.
When you look at the leader of  the Green Party you say “How can it be that Australia,
great Australia, is wealthier than New Zealand?”.
The ACT Party has had a great year in Parliament. No leadership spills, no
dissension, no waka jumping, and a united caucus—no waka jumping, no leadership
spills, and a united caucus. It is called stability for a John Key - led Government.
I want to say thank you very much to all of those people who make this place tick. I
want to thank the Speaker for his great ro le-model leadership. I want to thank you, my
old friend, for your role as Deputy Speaker of  this Parliament. None of us can do our
12 Dec 2012 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 7483
jobs without the officials around here and we  thank them for the smooth running of
Parliament.
The member for Epsom works hard for Epso m every day. On behalf of the people of
Epsom, can I thank my Epsom staff—Prisci lla, Brian, and Styan—for the great work
that they do. In the last 12 or 15 years 20,000 constituent inquiries have been dealt with
by that team, over the MMP period. To my Wellington team of Chris, Trish, Shelley,
David, Clodagh, Mark, Ella, and Louise, thank you very much to them. I was just
reflecting the other day how old I must be  getting. I was in the 1990 Jim Bolger
Government and now Jim Bolger’s grandda ughter works in my parliamentary office
here in Wellington. So it is a land of opportun ity and there is a place, as the leader of
“TAB First” will attest, for ageing politicians to make a difference in this Parliament.
Finally, I would like to say thank you to the ACT Party President, Chris Simmons,
my deputy leader, John Boscawen, and the thousands of ACT Party members up and
down this country.
I would also like to thank the Prime Minister for his generous consideration this year.
I have enjoyed working with the Prime Minister and his Cabinet team on those
significant Cabinet committees. I have very much enjoyed coming back and working
with the Prime Minister’s chief of staff,  my long-time friend Wayne Eagleson, and I
thank all of the Cabinet team for their support.
Thanks to the people of Epsom and thanks  to the ACT Party, we have no capital
gains tax, no printing money, no Soviet-sty le housing projects, no Russel Norman as
Minister of Finance, no 1970s national award - style labour laws, and we no longer have
the world’s most expensive emissions tradi ng scheme. That is what we do not have.
This is a great achievement. But that is not  just what we are about; we have achieved
much more than that. The ACT Party has in troduced legislation for partnership schools,
which will give those kids at the bottom 20 percent a chance to have the dignity of
work. We are pushing hard on the Resource Ma nagement Act, the job killing machine
that is stopping development and creating a tenant generation of young people. We will
have a much better Resource Management Ac t reform thanks to the ACT Party and
thanks to the leadership of Amy Adams and her team.
Mr Assistant Speaker Tisch, I look forward to 2013 as we have much more to do. I
wish you and everyone in Parliament, thei r friends, their family, and the wider
community—particularly the Epsom voters—of electors a very happy Christmas.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call the H on Peter Dunne—5
minutes.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: At times like this, one often
forgets that the real purpose of this type of speech is not so much to have an end-of-year
slanging match on the political issues of the year—although that happens—but to
acknowledge the support and give thanks to the people who make it possible for us to
be in this place and to do the job that we do. So I want to begi n immediately with my
votes of thanks, and then I will move on to some of the other issues as time permits.
Let me thank all of the people who work in  my office. I am not going to name them
all, because I have not got time to, but they do a great job, they are well appreciated, and
I value their support. I thank my electorat e staff, who handle many, many hundreds of
inquiries each year, many of which I never ge t to see because they are satisfactorily
resolved. I acknowledge also the work of the various Government departments around
this city, which help clear the backlogs and break through for so many of those people
in terms of the help that they need.
I want to thank all of the people who ma ke this Parliament run, Mr Assistant

items.speaker: Speaker
items.text: you and your fellow presiding offi cers, the Clerk’s Office, the select
committee office, the Cabinet Office, the Cabinet secretariat, the messengers, the
7484 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 12 Dec 2012
security guards, the people who run the cater ing service, our VIP drivers, our library
people, our research people, and all of our o fficials. Every single one of them makes an
important contribution to the smooth running of  this place and makes it possible for us
to be here representing the people of New Zealand.
I think that this year could be described as a typical first y ear of a second-term
Government. The gloss of the first 3 year s inevitably dulls somewhat. The real
challenges of Government become much  more apparent, and the mettle that
Governments are tested on is their ability to withstand t hose challenges and to forge a
path ahead. I think that this Government has done that admirably in extraordinarily
adverse circumstances this year. I think that  one of the other features of this year,
because of some of the partic ular events that have unfolde d, has been a rise in media
responsibility. I have usually been one who has been very critical of the media in New
Zealand. I thought that they have been superficial, but in reality I think that this year on
a number of issues they have performed thei r role admirably. I hope this might be the
start of a more permanent transition.
In terms of where New Zeala nd sits at the end of 2012, we  are still coming to grips
with the consequences of the worst econom ic depression since th e Great Depression.
Every day one hears more adverse news, not from New Zealand so much but from the
countries external to us that  will have an impact on us. For people to say that this
depression, this economic situation, is an ex cuse manufactured by the Government, just
like they say the earthquake s in Christchurch were an  excuse—oh that Governments
were so powerful to manipulate these things! The reality is that when you get news out
of Europe in the last week of fears of a triple-dip recession occurring within the
European Union, the bounce-back and flow-on to economies like New Zealand’s cannot
be avoided. That does not mean you give up the ghost. It does not mean you say it is all
beyond us. But what it does do is temper the level of response and temper the reality
within which Governments can operate.
This Government has done extremely well in those adverse circumstances. Look at
our debt-GDP ratio. Look at our unemploym ent, which is too high but by world
standards is still very much on the low side. Look at a number of the key indicators. We
are getting there, and the thing for New Zealand to remember, as 2012 draws to a close,
is that the way forward will not be achieved by  abrupt changes of path, and will not be
achieved by the implementation of policies that will actually shackle people’s
opportunity rather than create it. In respect of the debate about pove rty at the moment,
the one point that is being ignored is that  growth and opportunity are the way out of
poverty, not simply pouring more in the way of handouts.
So as we head off for our Christmas brea k, I want to conclude  on this point. For
many New Zealanders this will be a tough Christmas. I think we should acknowledge
them and just give them some space and some support at this time. For the rest of us, I
want to acknowledge the support and the encouragement—wry at times—of all
members of the House. I also want to wish  them and their families, whatever their
political persuasion, the very best of th e season ahead, good relaxation, good time with
family and friends, a reinvigora tion so that the debate about policy and issues next year
can be a full one, a charged one, a proper one, and an effective one. Merry Christmas to
all.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: In this very brief 5-minute call
I just want to join with others who have thanked the legions of people who make life
easy for us here in Parliament, and to add my sincere agreement with the sentiments that
have been expressed to this point. Anyone liste ning to this debate will pick up some of
the vitriol that is perhaps natu ral. It is the time of year when you reflect on a year gone,
and there is a great willingness and eagerne ss on the part of everybody to separate out
12 Dec 2012 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 7485
the differences between us all as politicians working for the betterment of New Zealand.
But I want to, just for a moment, put my ha t on as Leader of the House and make some
comments that are about the way in which the House has operated this year. I think
what many will not understand is that although there will be fierce debate on issues that
we have clear policy division on, there is a great deal  of work done in this place that is
simply for the betterment of New Zealanders, and there is a lot of legislation that has
passed through the House that a dds to the quality of life an d to the ease of doing your
daily business in this country that has agreement across the floor of the House.
There has been a lot of criticism over ma ny years about the way in which urgency
has been used, and I will not go into that, other than to say that at the beginning of the
2008 Parliament I put a notice of motion on th e Order Paper proposing that there might
be some change in the way in which some of that agreed business that the House deals
with could be handled. The Standing Orders Committee picked up that idea, and parties
from across the House wrote it into the Standi ng Orders for this Parliament. So we now
have this capacity for extended hours. The re sult of that this year has been that the
House has had only one session of urgency, appropriately around the Budget. It finished
at 6 o’clock on the Thursday night, meaning that there were no extra hours worked, but
the business was concluded satisfactorily.
We have had 12 sessions held under extended hours, with agreement by the Business
Committee, and one session held under ex tended hours by Government motion. The
Business Committee is a group convened by the Sp eaker. It has representatives from all
parties, and it works on near unanimity. In other words, if the representatives of the
greatest number of parliamentarians agree on something, it can happen. I want to pay
tribute to all members of the Business Co mmittee. I acknowledge Trevor Mallard as the
shadow Leader of the House fo r his contribution in changing  what I think has been the
way in which we sensibly look at business th at we are not divided on. Treaty settlement
bills are a perfect example. The progress that  is now being made, which really is the
fruition of many, many years of work acr oss different Governments, is, I think, a
splendid example of the way in which Parlia ment can work when these provisions are
used appropriately.
It also means that Parliament this year ha s sat for the equivalent of 35-plus weeks.
Given that our constitutional arrangements requi re us to sit for 30 weeks, that indicates
a very significant extra commitment from me mbers. So this has been a year when the
maturity of Parliament has come to fruition, and that is due to the senior members who
sit on that business community—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Committee.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: —and I think the whole Parliament should be proud of
them. I am not sure what Mr Mallard is sa ying, but he may be allowed 5 minutes at
some stage in this debate to make his thought s clear. Then again, in  a party that is so
divided as the Labour Party, a true parliamentarian like Trevor Mallard just does not get
a go.
Instead, we have to listen to the sort of drivel that we got from David Shearer. I want
to know how much the Labour Party paid to ha ve that speech wri tten. It was not his
material, he hardly knew it, he stumbled ove r his words, he did not get the punchlines,
and he had an audience behind him like a group  of trained seals, clapping and laughing
out of sequence. It was like watching a movie where it just sort of misses that cog in the
wheel, and you get the language and then the action coming in behind it.
Then there is poor old Winston Peters. I want  to say this to his group who were there
chanting behind him. We have seen two Parliaments full of New Zealand First chanters,
and not one of them is still here. So that is basically saying to the world “We’ll have
Winston.”, which means “We’re out of he re.”—gone. I now have to conclude, but I
7486 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 12 Dec 2012
want to thank you, Mr Speaker, as a presiding officer, and a ll presiding officers and the
Clerks for everything they do, as well.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The Hon Steven Joyce—5 minutes.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Could I also add
my thanks to all the people who work around this place for the work they have done in
the year that has just gone. As we head into Christmas, I think we should help the
Labour Party members ponder the big political  imponderable of the year—that is, if
2012 has been such a bad year for the Government, as they say it has, then why is it that
at the end of this year this Government is as  popular as it was at the start of the year? I
think you should ponder that over the barbecue at David Cunliffe’s over summer.
Actually, I can tell the Labour Party memb ers why they have this problem: it is
because they have no political credibility. Th ey have no credibility with the public and
they have no economic credibility. They thi nk the public are gullible,  and the reality is
the public are not gullible. The Labour Party members think they can argue that black is
white one day and white is black the next and nobody notices, but they cannot. They are
completely politically inconsistent. If they sold used cars they would give used-car
salesmen a bad name. They are in complete denial of the worst economic crisis the
world has seen for 80 years. That is their st arting point, to deny th at. As long as they
keep doing it, they are still going to keep fa lling over with the public. They act as if the
Government is not dealing with an earthquake . They say our growth  record is poor, yet
it is faster than most countries in the OECD —in fact, it is a lot fa ster than when they
were tossed out. They say New Zealand has a balance of payments problem, but our
balance of payments deficit is half the size it was when they were in charge.
They say New Zealand needs more savings, but we have actually got a positive
savings rate for the first time in 20 years. They say the cost of livi ng is too tough, and
yet real wages have grown over the last 4 years more than they did over the entire 9
years of the Labour Government. They say unemployment is a disaster, but 5,000 fewer
people are now on the unemployment benefit th an a year ago. They say manufacturing
is in a crisis, and yet volumes in manufacturi ng are up in the last year. They say exports
are down, but they are up. These people are in fantasyland. And the big news for them
is that the public is not buying it. They go on about jobs, and then they do not want the
Government to do anything about giving busin esses the opportunity to grow jobs. They
say we need more houses, and then yesterda y in this House they opposed the Resource
Management Act reforms that would speed up consents for houses.
Then it gets worse. Labour has no credibili ty, and then you add the Greens and it is
even worse. There is even less credibil ity and a lot less economic credibility. The
Greens argue for jobs and growth  and then oppose every single  thing that would lead to
real jobs and growth. Agriculture? No. Oil and gas? No—t here was little Gareth on the
front page of the Dominion Post this morning. Aquaculture? No. New coalmines? No.
Convention centres? No.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Did you hear what the
member said?

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The member must use a person’s
correct name. So when referring to the Green member, he must use the full name.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: So there was Gareth Hughes on the front page of the
Dominion Post this morning once again turning down oil and gas. So no new coalmines
and no convention centres. They are even opposed to just building a commercial
building.
More Chinese tourists? This one is courtesy of Winston—no. Johnny foreigner
investing in New Zealand? No, that is not  allowed. International education is not
allowed. Green jobs? Apparently, yes. So what  is a green job? It is a giant make-work
12 Dec 2012 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 7487
scheme. Here is a clue for Labour and the Greens. It is not an industry if there is nobody
wanting to invest in it except the taxpayer who is being forced to. It is not an industry; it
is a Ponzi scheme. It is giant make-work scheme, and we know where those end up.
They end up on the shores of the Mediterr anean Sea with Governments that have no
money. But that is all right; they can print the money. They just set up the printer and
they can print some more.
Labour members deny it, but actually they are the junior partner in this coalition with
the Greens. If it is such a good idea to print money why do the Greens not just go and
print off some carbon tax credits and solve climate change that way? It makes just as
much sense.
New Zealanders understand that  this Government is delivering in a tough world. We
are growing New Zealand. We are clawing our  way out of the global financial crisis,
and in fact we are doing better than most OECD countries. New Zealanders also know
that members on the other side have not ackno wledged the reality that the world is in
today, and they are never going to trust them while they do not acknowledge that
reality. New Zealanders are also saying th at these people have no solutions. Their
solutions are exactly the same as the old soluti ons, which is to promise all sorts of free
stuff with borrowed money.
Actually, the world has changed since then. You cannot promise free houses and
pretend you do not have to borrow money. It is  the same old bankrupt  visions. Frankly,
it is even more controlled by the political wing of the public sector unions. It is all about
the politics of patronage. The public are not buying it. Ponder that at David Cunliffe’s
barbeque this summer—the public are not buyi ng it, and if you keep going the way you
are going, they will not buy it for another year. Merry Christmas, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: This year has seen a decline in the National
Party’s credibility. It has also seen a rise in  the credibility of the Labour Party and in
particular of David Shearer. David Shearer’s  credibility has grown during the year and
most forcefully in the last month. I thought th at was apparent in the speech he gave in
the House today. It was a mature speech. It ha d humour in it. It was not forced. It the
sort of speech you would expect of a senior  politician. It was not, as the National Party
has tried to characterise it, some sort of jokey speech that was addressing trained seals
behind him. That was John Key’s attempt at humour, which, by contrast, was shallow.
I was asked earlier in the month what I t hought of David Shearer’s performance this
year. They asked me what his score was out of 10. I did not have quick answer at the
time, so I did really give a smart-arse answ er. I am not especially good at those. But I
did think about it afterwards. I thought: “What is the proper score for David Shearer out
of 10 this year?”. Well, I think it is between  seven and 11, because that is the narrowing
of the gap between National and Labour this ye ar. If we look at the worst of the polls,
the gap between National and Labour has narrowed by seven point s. If you look at the
better polls, the narrowing of the gap between National and Labour is by 11 points. The
gap is narrowing.
Why is that? Why is the National Party in de cline in its credibility? Well, it has been
a year of poor political management. It ha s been a year of scandal and mishap. The
Government has been diverted from paying attention to the prope r management of the
economy, and, as a consequence, we have a stagnant economy and we have record
numbers of people going to Australia. The list of scandals and mistakes is longer than I
have seen it since I have been in Parliament, and I have been here for a decade now. Just
a year ago we had the tea tapes. We had the Prime Minister using the power of the State,
disgracefully calling in the police against the media during an election. Lo and behold, a
month or two after the election they did not want to proceed with the prosecution,
because it would have been so embarrassi ng for the Prime Minister and John Banks to
7488 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 12 Dec 2012
turn up in court and pretend that their public stunt gone wrong was somehow an illegal
action on the part of the media, against whom the police were used. Then we had the
Prime Minister deeming Mr Ambrose guilty in  a way in which he would never even do
with John Banks, despite a written record showing that Mr Banks broke the law.
Then we had the ACC debacle. We had Ni ck Smith having to resign because he as
ACC Minister wrote a letter on behalf of Bronwyn Pullar advocating for her, and then
he misled the Prime Minister about having done so. So he had to fall on his sword. Then
we had mayhem in ACC. We had Judith Co llins kicking out the chair and losing the
chief executive. Most of the board went. We had privacy breaches—another scandal.
What was next? We had the centrepie ce of the Budget being improved student
outcomes through larger class sizes. What  a nonsense! That was the end of the
reputation of Hekia Parata, whose ignominy has been added to every time she stands up
in the House and fails in her duty to act co mpetently as a Minister. Yet she stays on as
the Minister of Education. Bring back the Minister of Police into that role is what—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I never thought I’d hear you say that.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: I never thought I would say that , Grant. But I saw that in a
column from one of the commentators recen tly, and I thought about how far the star of
Hekia Parata has fallen. That also besmirched  the reputation of the Minister of Finance,
because he was the other driver for that policy.
Then we had Murray McCully. Murray McCu lly and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs
and Trade—what a disaster that was! It was well brought to light by Phil Goff, who
showed that he is more than a match for Mr McCully.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: It’s a disgrace—maligning people in this House.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: I am maligning people in the House. I am maligning Mr
McCully because he was terrible.
Then we had pokie machines being traded for a convention centre. Then we had John
Banks, who sought donations, asked for them from Skycity, was given them personally
in an envelope, knew that they were fr om Skycity, and said they were anonymous.
Then, of course, we had the link with Dotcom and the fact that he said that he did not
know he had donations. That has already been covered by someone else. But the
Dotcom link then comes through in the next scandal that beset the National Party. A spy
agency, despite the fact that the residency for Dotcom was celebrated in the largest
display of fireworks ever, not just in Au ckland but in the whol e of New Zealand, and
that it was paid for by Dotcom, like the Keystone Cops, under Mr Key, missed it. Then
John Key forgot about it, and forgot about it again and again.
Meanwhile, what is happening to the economy? Well, the centrepiece of the
Government’s economic programme for this 3 years, asset sales, went off the rails.
Asset sales were meant to be the biggest part  of the economic plan for this country, for
this 3 years.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: We won. You lost.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: That is right. He says: “We won. You lost.” That is Simon
Bridges. New Zealanders lost. That hubris on the part of Simon will come back to haunt
him. Asset sales were never a cure for th e economic malaise of this country. Changing
who owned what already existed did nothing to increase the output of New Zealand. It
did not create one extra new job. All it di d was, over time, increase power prices—we
know that, because that was proven at th e select committee—and increase assets
inequality over time as those assets, inst ead of being owned by all New Zealanders,
would end up owned disproportionately by the same 10 percent of New Zealand that
this Government always acts for.
At Budget time we also had disclosure for the first time, which again showed Steven
Joyce to be the chief spinner for the National Party. He was rolled out at the time of the
12 Dec 2012 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 7489
last election to say that the Labour Party was telling lies wh en we said that we were
accounting for the proceeds of the asset sale s, but were not accounting for the loss of
share of profits. Sure enough, come the Bu dget the Government had to admit it—a
deficit that was $100 million per annum worse because of asset sales.
In the meantime what has happened to the economy? Well, the Government
promised that people could say goodbye to higher taxes, not their loved ones. That is
what the National Party was elected on in 2008. What has ha ppened since? There have
been record levels of people leaving New Zealand for Australia—the highest ever in the
history of New Zealand. More than 175,000 have left since National took office. That is
more than the population of Hamilton, it is  more than the population of Napier and
Hastings combined, and it is more than the population of Dunedi n and Invercargill
combined. Some areas have lost 4 per cent of their population—4 percent of their
population. Despite that record loss of people, we have got unemployment at the highest
rate in 13 years—over 7 pe rcent. What did the unemp loyment numbers do? They
surprised the Government. Gove rnment members said that they thought that it was
inconsistent, yet the banks had already forecas t it going to over 7 percent. The quarterly
employment survey had also shown an increase in unemployment.
We have had an increase in child poverty a nd inequality. I do not have time to cover
that, but I am sure my colleague Jacinda Ardern will do that justice. We have had
exports down. The Government says there is no crisis in manufacturing. Well, it is true
that primary manufacturing holds up when te rms of trade go against you—that is true.
But non-primary manufacturing really suffers, and that is  what is suffering. We are
losing jobs in that sector. This Government refuses to pull the leve rs of power that are
open to it. The Government says that the La bour Party stands for nothing. We stand for
a neutral investment signal that is fair, th rough a capital gains tax, and that also
improves the economy. We stand for universal  KiwiSaver and changes to the Reserve
Bank of New Zealand Act so that the Reserv e Bank does not give primacy to inflation
targeting over things like the exchange rate and full employment.
The last thing I would say is that the me ssaging of the Government is now becoming
desperate. For years it said that we in Labour  were fiscally irrespons ible, then just this
week we have got John Key saying there were $20 billion of surpluses in 3 years under
Labour, and because of that we did not sp end enough on child poverty. Despite the fact
that we lifted many people out of child pove rty through Working for Families, the truth
is we were responsible fiscally. We have pa rtially rehabilitated our reputation in respect
of fiscal responsibility this year. We left the lowest Government debt in the world and
the lowest unemployment in the world, a nd this Government has squandered that
advantage.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I am proud to stand here as a member
of the New Zealand National Party caucus and a Minister in a National-led Government.
Why? Because this Government delivers. De spite some of the most difficult economic
times since the 1930s, the New Zealand economy is in better shape now than it was in
2008 when we took over from that lot over there. Why? Firstly, because we have a
fantastic leader who, by the way, can write his own speeches, and we have a united
caucus.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: We’ve got a fantastic finance Minister as well.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I was just going to say we have got a fantastic finance
Minister. He can add up, and he can subtract  and multiply, which is more than we can
say for them over there. Will you stop taking my lines, Mr Bridges.
We have got strong, clear plans to st rengthen our economy. We are supporting
Christchurch and the rebuild of Christchur ch. We have supported the elderly and some
of New Zealand’s most vulnerable through these tough times. We are focused on
7490 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 12 Dec 2012
delivering Better Public Services. In othe r words, we are working hard for New
Zealanders, but we are working smarter and better.
What a great year our New Zealand Police have had. There is a 5.9 percent drop in
the crime rate, and that is on top of a 7 per cent drop in the crime rate last year. What a
fantastic job they are doing, rolling out Polic ing Excellence, which includes things like
Prevention First, which is getting out and working in the communities. There are 33
neighbourhood policing teams working in some  of our most hard-hit crime areas,
working with communities to stop crime fr om happening. The better use of technology
sees our officers not having to go back into the station so mu ch, and that is how we are
delivering more front-line policing hours than ever before, and that is making a real
difference in our communities. I would like to  thank all of our pol ice staff, sworn and
non-sworn, up and down the country. They are brave people. They are extremely patient
people. They are ultimate professionals. I wish them all a very merry Christmas.
What about the Department of Corrections ? Well, it has seen a 5 percent drop in
reoffending rates. What does that mean? That actually means this year we have seen
3,700 fewer victims of crime, and about 925 fewer offenders. I think that has made a big
difference in some of our communities. We  have rolled out more education, more
training and skills, and more alcohol and drug rehabilitation to more prisoners than ever
before. Even in these tough economic times we  have been putting education in front of
remand prisoners, which has never been done before. We are making a real difference to
turning round the lives of some of these pr isoners. I think our prison officers and our
corrections staff have done a magnificent j ob this year. I want to put on record our
thanks to them, and wish them a merry Christmas too.
In addition we have the Seri ous Fraud Office. Its job is to bring those white-collar
criminals to justice. It also has had a fantastic year with prosecutions and cases before
the courts. Serious Fraud Offi ce staff are the ones who are ge tting those guys into court
and making them take ownership and be re sponsible for all those people out in New
Zealand whom they have scammed out of thei r life-savings. They have got those white-
collar criminals brought to jus tice. I want to thank all of  those staff who work in
Auckland in particular, and wish them a merry Christmas.
While we are wishing everyone a merry Ch ristmas, can I wish Mr Speaker, the
Deputy Speaker, and the Assistant Speakers a merry Christmas. Thank you for your
presiding over this House throughout the year. Can I add my thanks to all the staff who
work in the precincts of Parliament, the Cl erks, the Hansard people, the messengers, the
cleaners, the security people, and the people who work in Bellamy’s and down here in
the cafeteria. Can I thank my fabulous staff. Can I wish to all the members of this House
safe journeys, safe celebrat ions, safe swimming and boati ng, and enjoy a New Zealand
summer. Kia ora.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call Todd McClay—5 minutes.

items.speaker: TODD McCLAY
items.text: Um, um, um. Ah, ah, ah. Um, um, um.
Anybody who is listening to this on the radio at  the moment probably thinks the Leader
of the Opposition, David Shearer, is on his feet speaking again. This is the year that he
has limped from one um and one ah to another, all the way through the whole year.
Do you remember at the beginning of the y ear when they were about to have their
caucus meeting not far from Taup ō? He stood beside a dairy farm and he ummed and
ahhed and said that no longer would these farms be able to be sold to foreigners. Then
when he was asked about the details he umme d and he ahhed some more, and of course
we do not see a bill in his name before this House that is going to deal with this issue.
Just a very short time ago when he was as ked whether or not he  had the full support
of his caucus I thought he was counting them on the ums and the ahs because there were
so many when he was put in front of the television cameras. But what we do know is
12 Dec 2012 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 7491
now absolutely he does have them all. A nother um and another ah there. He came
forward with the big strategy to turn round the wayward direction of the Labour Party at
its conference this year. Wh at happened when he was asked about how the houses
would come about? All we got for those poor  New Zealanders who want a house was
more ums and more ahs.
Can I say this has been a good year for th e Government because the Government is
focused on what is important for New Zealande rs and what the really important things
are that we must do for this country. This is a year when a hard-working Government
has done more and achieved more than any year that many in this House can remember.
Do you know what this year is? This is the year of The Hobbit. The Green Party has
been here almost every year saying to us in this House that it is in favour of labelling.
Well, that is a film that is going round th e world—released in cinemas this week—that
has a label on it that says “Made in New Zealand”. This is the year of The Hobbit .
Thank goodness that Gerry Brownlee and John Key secured that film and future films
for New Zealand. Thank goodness they secured 3,000 jobs for New Zealand and work
for 3,000 businesses. Members opposite in th e Labour Party laugh and scoff because
they wanted this to be the year of the  Hobbit-haters. They did not want the film to have
“Made in New Zealand” on it. They did not want that film to be made here. They
wanted to back their union mates and Au stralian unions so 3,000 New Zealanders
would not have jobs and 3,000 businesses would not have work to do on this important
industry. I say again thank goodness for J ohn Key and Gerry Brownlee and the work
they did for everyday New Zealanders, who are proud that film has been made here.
What has this Government done this year in an extremely hard-working year? We
heard from the Prime Minister earlier that th e deficit has been halved over what it was
last year and we are on track back to surp lus, something that would not have happened
under a Green-Labour coalition Government if  it was on this side of the House this
year. We have got the lowest interest ra tes in New Zealand for 50 years. Again
members opposite scoff and laugh, but mums and dads out there who are paying
mortgages on houses—that actually are re al houses, not the 100,000 those members are
pretending they will magic up from thin air—are glad about th is because of the
economic management of Bill English as the Minister of Finance.
Since we have been here in this Parliament there have been 60,000 new jobs. Some
of those jobs have come with Australian  companies to New Zealand. The Opposition,
the Labour Party, stood up in New Zealand an d said that they are the wrong types of
jobs and they do not pay enough. Well, here is  the thing: if you look around the world a
job is a job and it is a good job. This Gove rnment backs New Zealanders and backs
those jobs. We are glad that Australian co mpanies have brought jobs here because they
have confidence in the direction the Government is going in.
I turn to roads around  New Zealand and infrastructure . I was horrified to hear a
member of the Opposition who is in the Waik ato area—I think in your electorate, Mr
Assistant Speaker Tisch—saying that she was against a very important road in the Bay
of Plenty, the Te Puke bypass, which goes from my electorate through Tony Ryall’s
electorate to the Port of Tauranga in Simon Bridges’ electorate. That is what—

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: What’s it called?

items.speaker: TODD McCLAY
items.text: They say it is the Te Puke bypass.  That is what they are saying.
They do not back important roads anywhere in New Zealand. They do not back
important roads in the Bay of Plenty that will add productivity a nd jobs to our local
economy.
In crime, there has been a 5.9 percent drop in crime rates in New Zealand. That is a
fantastic job on the part of our Ministers and our police.
7492 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 12 Dec 2012
In the moment, the minute, I have got left I want to thank the staff of the Finance and
Expenditure Committee, which I get to chair. I want to thank the staff of Parliament. I
want to thank the members of the comm ittee. I want to thank you, Mr Assistant
Speaker, and to Lockwood Smith I wish him the very best for a successful holiday
period and 2013. I will end here, Mr Assistant Speaker. A little bit of advice—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Sorry to interrupt the member, his
time has expired.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I am not sure just what  happened there in that
speech, but I want to start at  the beginning of mine by a dding my thanks to all the
wonderful staff who make this place what  it is, who keep it ticking along, and who,
basically, put up with all of us existing in this space, particularly the forbearance of
those who have to listen to all of our speech es here in this Chamber. I want to add my
special thanks to the Labour team and extended wh ānau and all the work that they do—
our research unit, our media team, the leader’s office, and all of our executive assistants.
They are very special people, and I know I speak for my colleagues when I thank them
sincerely for their work.
John Key stood up as Prime Minister in this  House and in his adjournment debate
speech claimed that he had ended the year as  he had started. That  literally, actually,
cannot be true. Based on some of the facts that  we have before us, things are actually
much, much worse than even when he star ted this year. And you know that things are
bad, things are terrible, when a Government starts, in order to try to prove that things
are OK, comparing its statistics and its figures  with the 1990s and the last time that it
was having an absolutely dismal time in G overnment. Not for everyone has this been a
positive year. In fact, for the majority of Kiwis, particularly those who are most
vulnerable, including some of our youngest me mbers of society, this has been a very
difficult year, and there is no bright light on the horizon.
It is telling that on the forecourt of Parlia ment today, this last sitting day, the Child
Poverty Action Group’s youth wing—and I congr atulate it on its in itiative and its
work—organised a rally on Parliament calle d “Bare your soles for child poverty”. It
asked that for a brief moment  politicians take off their shoes and experience what many

items.speaker: Kiwi kids are experiencing on a daily basis
items.text: basic material deprivation. I do not say that
in a flippant way. We know the figures. Ma terial deprivation has gone from 15 percent
to 21 percent under this Government. Thos e are basic enforced lacks—not having
enough money to go to the doctor and fill you r prescription, so forgoing doctors’ visits
when you are sick. That would explain the incr ease in preventable hospitalisations that
we have seen in this country, and the Children’s Social Health Monitor  released this
week showed us that.
The shame that this Government needs to face up to is things like Third World
diseases, rheumatic fever, infectious skin diseases, and kids ending up in hospital
because their eczema has got so bad, or because they have things like scabies but do not
even have enough hot water or power in their homes to do a hot wash to get rid of it.
This is Third World stuff, and this our national shame—the National Party’s shame. We
have 270,000 children living in poverty. These are our most vulnerable children, despite
what Ms Bennett said when she produced her white paper that was meant to help
vulnerable children, then narro wed down the number she wanted to help to a few,
10,000 or 20,000. There are 270,000 children w ho need this House’s attention—
270,000. One in five children is growing up in the homes of parents who are reliant on
Government support, of parents who are on be nefits because they cannot find work and
they have an inadequate income to survive on. That is this Government’s legacy. That is
how it is ending this year, and I see no bright  light in the forthcoming years to remedy
that. For our kids, it has been an epic fail of a year.
12 Dec 2012 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 7493
Many—and I understand this—have asked us on this side of the House, and have
asked the Greens and asked the Mana Pa rty, “Why can’t you collaborate with the
Government to try to resolve this situati on for our most vulnerable kids?”. I answer
them sincerely and frankly that we cannot lo wer our sights as low as that Government
has set the bar. We cannot aim that low, an d until that Government raises the bar for
what it will do for those children, we cannot  and will not collabora te with such low
aspirations for children. But I know what that Government will say. I can hear it now. It
will say that it has brought in its welfare re forms. That has been its response to child
poverty. Show me how the Government has helped one child with its welfare reforms. I
will tell you what they do. There is not one extra training opportunity in that bill. There
is not one new job. There are more sanctions . We have already seen them. They have
doubled under this Government to 57,000 per annum, and 377 families have had their
benefits cut by this Government. How has that helped child poverty, I ask it.
There is more work testing, but no more wo rk. There are more obligations, but again
no response from the Government as to how it is going to improve people’s chances of
getting employment. It is contracting out medical assessments. We have already got a
chief medical assessor, who likens Governme nt support to a drug. Where is the dignity
in social security when you have someone w ho uses references like that? It has put in
what it calls its social obligations, yet as a Government it shows no obligation to help
Kiwis find employment—the most basic of ro les for a Government. I imagine that what
the Government will also throw up is that it has had the odd target in health. Well, that
is all very well, but the Government continues to treat the symptoms and not the cause.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: A huge improvement.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: Why try to swab for rheumatic fever, Mr Calder, when you
could spend a few thousand dollars insula ting a house and save yourself tens of
thousands of dollars down the track? Why not treat the overcrowded housing and the
poor provision of social housing in this country ? In fact, let us go back to basics. Why
not measure poverty? Why not measure povert y? This Government has refused to do
even that. When you have a Prime Minister who says that what gets measured gets
done, and that you will not know whether you are successful unless you measure it, you
know there is no intention to deal with our national shame, because the Government
refuses to measure poverty. Unicef, the OECD—e veryone else seems to manage it, but,
as Richie Poulton from Otago University has pointed out, we have Third World diseases
and we have Third World data. That needs to change.
That brings me to my final point. If that Government does not want to help
vulnerable children as a moral imperative, maybe it will look at it as an economic one.
We spend $6 billion to $8 billion per annum  on child poverty, yet the Government will
not reprioritise what we spend in order to prevent children from having a miserable start
in life as a consequence. There are things  we can do, and Labour has already presented
part of its plan. Firstly, let us demons trate our accountability. Let us legislate a
requirement to measure the five measures of  poverty: relative meas ures, static income
measures, material deprivation, severity, and persistence. Let us measure it. Then let us
set targets to reduce it. I have a bill that  the Government could pick up tomorrow if it
wanted. I am not telling the Government how much it has to reduce it by; I am just
telling it that it should at least aspire to do it. It is as basic as that. We should also be
transparent about how much we have achie ved: tell the public; re port on child poverty.
What a difference, I have no doubt, that would make. We urge the Government: surprise
us, take up that bill in its name, and legislate to be accountable on child poverty.
Secondly, put food in schools. It is basic. It  is a no-brainer. For the Government to
claim that it is doing its part because it has got food parcels shows how desperate things
are. Put food in schools. There is no reason,  regardless of whether that Government
7494 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 12 Dec 2012
wants to blame parents or others, that children should suffer as a result of the
Government’s principle on food in schools. Thirdly, adopt our policy of warrants of
fitness for rental properties. Not all of the kids living in poverty are in State houses—in
fact, the majority are not. They are cold, they are damp, and they deserve better from us,
and we can and should set some standards fo r them. Finally, income  matters. You will
not solve child poverty unless we look at income. The mini mum wage needs to go up,
and we need a living wage. These are just the beginning of things that Labour would do
in Government on behalf of kids.
Next year must be the year for our ki ds. Despite Maggie Barry’s standing orders—
we may not have experienced poverty in this  House—it is absolute ly our responsibility
to do something about it. This Labour Part y when in Government  will. Until then, we
watch shamefully as that Government stands idly by and does nothing.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Mr Speaker, my very
merry Christmas wishes to you and everyone in this precinct. I am sad to say that that is
about as much Christmas cheer as you are going to get out of me this afternoon, because
the reality is that we have heard some appalling speeches from the other side of the
House. We had an angry little  speech from Ms Ardern over there, who seems to have
absolutely no concept of where money comes from or the fact that we have had a global
financial crisis. We have been dealing w ith that as best we  can, and, actually, our
numbers are holding up excepti onally well. We have had fr om Metiria Turei over there
a rendition—the long version—of her Christ mas holidays over the years. I have not
quite worked out the actual reason for that. We have heard from David Parker, who has
given us his score of his l eader, between 7 and 11. I am not  quite sure why he gave a
range, but I think it is because he is no longer sure of his numbers.
But I think the real story this year politically inside this House is an absolute contrast
between a party on this side that is soberly and correctly getting on with the business—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Soberly? Isn’t Maggie Barry on your side?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Well, I am not talking about you, Trevor. It gets on with
the business of Government, in the worst economic times for many, many years, with
good numbers, and there is a shambles on th e other side over there, the Opposition,
which cannot work out what is going on and wh ich seems to be caught up in sideshows,
personality disputes, and egos.
Let us start with the Labour Party. Of cour se, we know that it has had a leadership
contest between David and David. I do not want to dwell on that . As interesting as it is,
it is old ground. But here is th e real issue: Labour Party members changed their rules,
they had a vote, and they have entrenched a loser as their leader. They have entrenched
a loser as their leader. That is what they ha ve done. The real stor y is that they hated
Cunliffe so much—they hated him so much—t hat they decided they had to stick with
the loser that they have got.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: You wait and see.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Annette King says: “You wait and see.” Well, here is what
Labour Party lovey Judy Callingham—who is married to one Brian Edwards and who is
a friend, a personal friend I would say, to the members opposite—said very recently, as
quoted by the New Zealand Herald : “… broadcasting guru Ian Fraser has ‘done
wonders for his speech-making’ ”—this is about David Shearer—“ ‘but no voice or
media coach can change the brain patterns, a nd that’s what’s affecting his non-scripted
material.’ ” It is the brain patterns, the synapses going between his brain.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Does Simon have any of those? Any brain patterns at all?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: What was Judy Callingham talking about? Let me put this
simply for Trevor Mallard. Labour Party lovey Judy Callingham was painting the real
picture when it comes to David Shearer: he is thick. He is thick, and they are stuck with
12 Dec 2012 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 7495
him, due to their hatred of Cunliffe. So I say to the Labour Party: “Look, do anything.
Do something in February. Change your lead er. Go Grant. Go Annette as a caretaker
leader. But don’t stick with the loser that you’ve got, because he is a loser who’s got
problems with his synapses.”
While we are on it, let us go to some of the other parties. There is the Green Party,
and the real leader of the Green Party is Russel Norman, ladies and gentlemen. He is
doing so well with his “bluewas h”—with his sensible, moderate, and financially literate
discussion. But the hubris got to him, he coul d not help it, and s uddenly he is talking
about the funny money—he is talking about th e funny money. Then the real beauty that
will come back to that party is that he decided in the thrill of the moment that he would
make it quite clear that he wa nts to be Minister of Finan ce. He wants to be deputy
leader. He had a dream and that is what he wanted.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: The angry Simon won’t get into Cabinet.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: What is very clear to me is that that soft support in Mount
Eden and the Khandallahs—probably wher e Grant Robertson lives—and the middle-
class housewives will be scared by this guy as Minister of Fi nance. That is the way it is
going.
Then, of course, we have the New Zealand First Party—
Le’aufa’amulia Asenati Lole-Taylor: What a good party, that one.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: —and the issues with Brendan. We will see where that
goes. Brendan Horan says he represents the people of Tauranga. Well, let me tell you,
Asenati, he does not represent the people of Tauranga, OK? The people who voted for
him, they voted for him because they thought  he was Winston’s son, OK? They thought
he was Winston’s son, but that is not where it  is going. So on this side we have a party
that is focusing on the real issues and getting on with business, and we have sideshows,
personality disorders, and egos on that side.

items.speaker: NICKY WAGNER
items.text: After a couple of tough
years the people of Christchur ch, at the end of 2012, are feeling increasingly positive
about our future. We know that, because in  a recent survey Christchurch people are
leading the way in wanting to stay in th eir home town. Ninety-seven percent of
Christchurch business people and 88 percent of Christchurch residents want to stay in
