Christchurch, which compares with only 86 percent of people across the country.
We are very optimistic, and it  is not surprising. We have the biggest growth rate and
the lowest unemployment rate in the count ry, and 78 percent of our business people say
that Christchurch is going in the right di rection, as do 61 percent of our residents,
against 51 percent of the people across the country.
Of course, we are deeply sad for those whom we have lost and for what we have lost,
but we now have a strong vision for the future  and are determined to make the most of
every opportunity. We are proud of how our communities have responded to the
disaster, and although we know there is stil l a long way to go, we feel challenged and
energised by the work ahead.
Most of us now know the fate of our homes . Many of us are alre ady on the path to
repair, rebuild, or replacement, and some ar e already through the process. In fact, at
least 30,000 homes have been rebuilt or repaired, and of ten those outcomes are much
better than we ever expected or dare d to hope for. Earthquake Commission and
insurance problems are still challenging for many. The Earthquake Commission is an
organisation that we love to hate, but we are all grateful that because of the commission,
99 percent of New Zealanders are insured, $4 b illion has been paid out in Christchurch,
and all of the 620,000 earthquake claims will be met.
Local community plans are working forward, and new suburban shops, cafe, and
community buildings are going up across the city, and in the central business district the
7496 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 12 Dec 2012
Christchurch City rebuild and blueprint based on the city council’s Share an Idea
consultation has been very well received. Awa reness of the plan is high and, for those
who are well informed, 82 percent of business people and 66 percent of residents
approve it and support it.
I want to take the opportunity right now to thank the Prime Minister and Gerry
Brownlee for their support and to thank the G overnment for its total commitment to the
rebuild of Christchurch, especially the $13 b illion that is going to be invested in our
future. We are incredibly fortunate that the Prime Minister came from Christchurch,
because he understands our community absolu tely. He understands it is important as a
gateway to the South Island and understa nds its contribution to the New Zealand
economy.
But it is actually Gerry Brownlee’s day in, day out leadership, his integrity in making
difficult and complex decisions, and his ability to think clearly and realistically in an
emotionally charged and ever-changing enviro nment that have delivered so well for
Christchurch and Canterbury. Again, Gerry has been the figure that we have loved to
hate, but as time goes by, more and mo re Cantabrians are understanding and
appreciating his tough but fair decision-making.
In the future I believe that Christc hurch people will look back on the great
earthquakes of 2010 and 2011 and will thank Ge rry and this Government for a steady
hand and intelligent and compassionate solu tions. As the member of Parliament for
Christchurch Central, an electorate that wa s hard hit in the earthquakes, I am proud of
the progress that we are making and of the r ecovery of our city, and I am enthusiastic
about our future. We will build a stronger, more sustainable, fabulously people-friendly
and prosperous city. Happy Christmas to  everyone and a great New Year, and no
earthquakes, please.

items.speaker: DENISE ROCHE
items.text: Ngā mihi nui ki a koe . Ki te Whare, t ēnā koutou katoa.
It is my privilege to take this last call of the year in the House for the Greens, and I am
delighted, because today is a very auspicious day. Today it is the 12 th of the 12 th of the
12th, and today the asteroid Toutatis will buzz the Earth, coming to within 4.4 million
miles of the planet. This asteroid app ears every 4 years and you can see it with a
telescope. Apparently, it has nothing to do with the Mayan calenda r and the predicted
end of the world next week, but more about that later.
It does not sound that close, at 4.4 milli on miles, but actually that asteroid is
probably closer to Earth than the Govern ment’s economic policy is to improving the
economy. Here on planet Earth we have got a Prime Minister this year with memory
lapses and brain fades, who describes his mo st desirable place, “Planet Key”, as having
no toilets. As a woman who has had a couple of  children, all I can say is that I am in
awe of that man’s pelvic floor muscles.
Of course, the Prime Minister is not the only one who has had memory problems this
year. The entire parliamentary caucus of  the ACT Party—the Hon John Banks—forgot
a lot of things, including two very large donations from a very large, German-born New
Zealand resident with the very memorable name of Kim Dotcom.
But back to the number 12. According to numerology—and I qualify this by saying
that although I do have long hair and I do play the guita r and I do live on Waiheke
Island, I am not a hippie, and I do not believe in numerology. However, according to
numerology, the number 12 is very auspicious. It is the number, and I quote, “attributed
to the government of the world or the cosmos .” Go figure. I believe that, for me, the
number 12 is very auspicious, because I am number 11 on the Green Party list, and, as
well as that, we got just under 12 percent of the vote at the last election.
These are very auspicious times becaus e next Friday, 21 December 2012, marks the
end of the Mayan calendar. I consulted the oracle, Google, and what it says about it is
12 Dec 2012 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 7497
that “The Ancient Mayan calendar speaks of  21-12-2012 as being th e end of times as
we know it, and the beginning of a new cycl e of evolution for planet earth, humanity,
and the cosmos.” You know, it is worth no ting that the predictions from the Mayan
calendar have been shown to be more accu rate than the teachers’ payroll system.
Anyway, according to the oracle,  Google, Mayan elders say that “the Ancients were
informing the modern world to be ready fo r a giant transformation for the human race.
Interestingly, traditions across the worl d including Buddhism, Tao, Hopi and Vedic
knowledge predict a ‘Golden Age’ … in their calendars around the same period.”
I was stoked when I read that. I t hought: “Yay! We’re coming up for another
election.” Or maybe it means there is somethi ng spiritual that is going to happen in the
House. Will the Minister for Economic Deve lopment be suddenly overcome with a fit
of compassion? Will the Minister for Social  Development begin to recognise and care
for needy children? Will the Minister responsible for digging toxic stuff out of the
ground and polluting the air with  it suddenly find fulfilment in his soul from organic
gardening? Will the Minister of Local Gove rnment wake up and find he actually does
believe in local government? Will the earthquake Minister finally give the people of
Christchurch a fair go and maybe some of their democracy back? Maybe the National
Government will finally do something about climate change.
In the new enlightenment and the season ahead, we the Green Party will welcome the
newly enlightened into the fold, after a suitab le period of re-education in the forest with
someone wise and knowledgable—perhaps some one like Jeanette Fitzsimons. So, from
the Greens, we wish everyone all the best for this coming season of peace and goodwill,
and we are hoping for a more enlightened Parliament next year.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Dr Cam Calder—5 minutes.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: As the waves of the ongoing financial turmoil
continue to lap relentlessly on the shores of  New Zealand, New Zealanders give thanks
to this National-led Government. They r ecognise that we provide the prudent,
pragmatic, and fiscal financial management that these troubled times demand. IMF
Managing Director Christine Lagarde has ur ged policy makers in all countries to
maintain crisis management mode as the global economy experiences a wide decline of
confidence and problems mount in the eurozone and beyond.
Just last week US Secretary of the Tr easury Timothy Geithner warned that the
domestic dithering continues and that he coul d not guarantee that th e fiscal cliff would
be averted. This could lead to  a potential hit in the US GDP of 3 percent to 5 percent.
President of the European Central Bank Mario Draghi has said he would do whatever it
takes to hold the eurozone together, but the eurozone’s recession shows no signs of
easing. In China, growth appears to have slow ed to just over 7 percent as politicians
struggle to accelerate the shift from an expor t-driven economy to one that relies on
domestic consumption. Globally, then, growth  could stutter in 2013,  should any of the
Opposition be concerned.
Here in New Zealand we are reducing our exposure to overseas debt markets as
much as possible, while still cushioning vul nerable New Zealanders from the harshest
edges of the ongoing financial crisis. New Z ealand’s economy, it s hould be noted, is
performing better than the ec onomies of the US, Japan, Germany, France, and the UK,
and growth in the last quarter is on a par w ith that of Australia. We have focused on
growth that is sustainable and built on highe r savings and earnings, rather than ever-
increasing consumption and debt, as exampled by the previous Government.
Our policies to navigate this fiscal fog of uncertainty are prudent, practical, and
precise, and have received a ringing endorseme nt from Peter Orszag, more recently US
President Obama’s Director of the Office of  Management and Budget. Orszag praised
New Zealand as standing out in the world as the only country that has coupled
7498 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 12 Dec 2012
additional economic stimulus with medium-ter m fiscal consolidation. Not surprisingly,
huge numbers of New Zealanders suffer ni ghtmares at the thought of our measured
approach being replaced by an economy managed by a coalition of Green, abacus-
hugging, parallel universe, ersatz  economists and their spendt hrift, lacklustre, Labour
union lackey colleagues.
Our astute financial management has led to our being able to  cushion the most
vulnerable from the worst effects of this ongoi ng crisis. Nowhere is this more evident
than in the health and social development portfolios. As a member of the Health
Committee I had the pleasure of attending a global health forum recently where many
delegates complained about th e effects of the global financ ial crisis on their health
budgets. In 2009-10 in this country, whilst other OECD countries were reducing
spending, New Zealand had a 3.4 percent incr ease in real health  spend—the third-
highest of 27 nations.
In my maiden speech I spoke of how a count ry is judged by how it treats its most
vulnerable, and I observed that a Government  cannot legislate aroha and a Government
cannot legislate love. The White Paper fo r Vulnerable Children sets out this
Government’s commitment to identify, s upport, and protect the 20,000 to 30,000 most
vulnerable children in our society. Decade afte r decade the deaths of up to a dozen of
our most vulnerable kiddies annually has been  a stain on our nation’s escutcheon. This
Government is doing something about it, informed by 10,000 submissions on a green
paper. The white paper sets out how this  Government will a ddress the appalling
incidence of these tragic events.
In the last week I have spoken in nine towns and communities all over New Zealand,
from Napier to Invercargill, on this multi-st randed initiative. The implementation of the
Children’s Action Plan will be driven by ke y Ministers in Wellington, and implemented
by the chief executives of social developmen t, health, justice, education, housing, Te
Puni K ōkiri, and the police. They will work t ogether to be jointly accountable for
achieving results for our vulnerable childr en. The joint accountability is hugely
significant. No longer will these tragedies be swept under Child, Youth and Family’s
front door. Key features of th e plan are a Vulnerable Kids Information System, a risk
predictor tool, and the devel opment of a stand-alone, neutral Child Protect line. These
initiatives are crucial, long overdue, and possible only because of our prudent and
thoughtful fiscal rectitude.

items.speaker: NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I am very pleased to speak in this
adjournment debate. Can I start by acknow ledging you, Mr Speaker. I do believe that
you have been one of the best Speakers in th e history of this Parliament. I want to
acknowledge you for your consistent patien ce, your grace, and your good humour. I
want to wish the parliamentary precincts a merry Christmas—even the media. I also
want to acknowledge some of my constituents  in this House: David Cunliffe, Denise
Roche, and Winston Peters. My office is alwa ys open, if you have any issues that you
want to chat about.
We are 4 years into this National Governme nt, and what is clear today? We have
heard many a speech about credibility. But wh at credibility is about is not rewriting
history; what credibility is about is delivering for New Zeal anders with costed policies
that will make a difference to this countr y. We were handed “Mi ssion: Impossible”. In
Labour’s last year of office we were hande d an economy with high inflation. We were
handed unemployment that grew by 30,000. Labour had committed us to badly costed
policies such as hundreds of millions of dollars paid for KiwiRail, and ACC blowouts in
terms of liabilities. We then had the deepest recession in a generation, and then we were
hit by several tragedies, including Pike  River and the Canterbury earthquakes.
Canterbury alone hit our country—$30 billion has been the cost so far.
12 Dec 2012 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 7499
What have we done? We have  done everything we can, da y in and day out, to be
fiscally responsible and work hard for our country. Our economy is growing at 2.6
percent. We are on track to return to surp lus. We have halved our deficit from $18
billion to $9 billion. Ther e are 65,000 net new jobs, and 13,000 jobs created by the 90-
day trial period. But what is clear is that  Opposition members are living in a bubble,
where they are divided, and they are in denial. They are still releasing uncosted policies.
David Shearer sits there, and I have a fe w questions for Mr Shearer. I come from
Auckland. I have a lot of young people in my electorate who would like to get into a
house. But what is clear is that when  Labour announced its housing affordability
package it was not only unaffordable but al so did not even contain houses. I went
looking in my electorate for tracts of land that were worth $50,000. I did find some,
actually. They were the third an d fourth floors of the Victor ia Street car-park. That is
where the Labour Party is in terms of hous ing affordability. We need to do more. We
must increase the supply of land. We must do more around resource management
processes. But what was absolutely incredible  was that yesterday in  the House, at the
first chance the Opposition had to support so me things around housing affordability, it
voted them down. There were two key provi sions: one around the Auckland Plan, and
the other around medium consents for many subdivisions in New Zealand. We saw it
have an epic fail at the first hurdle.
When it comes to looking after our most vulne rable, it has been tough for so many
New Zealanders, but what I can tell you is th at we have ensured that entitlements are
kept, we have increased New Zealand supe rannuation, and we have implemented more
than 30 initiatives to help some of our mo st vulnerable and at-risk children. We have
established seven teen parent units. We have put in $15 million more to ensure
vulnerable teen parents get th e right support that they nee d. Within our welfare reforms
we have established a guaranteed childcare assistance payment so that childcare costs
do not stop young parents from studying. When it comes to policies being costed,
whether it is from an economic perspective, Resource Management Act reform, or
infrastructure investment, or when it comes to helping our most vulnerable, our record
is clear in the most difficult time period in a generation. Whether it has been the deepest
recession, the hit by Canterbury, Pike River, or the fact that we have had to account for
all of these blowouts, we ha ve been delivering both from an economic perspective and
for our most vulnerable.
If you contrast that, you have an Oppositio n that is focused on slogans and on each
other, and that is divided. What I am conf ident about is that not only do we have a
Prime Minister who cares and who has deliv ered more for this country in a very
difficult period but also we have a united Na tional caucus with costed policies that is
ready to continue to deliver and to do the best that we can for New Zealanders.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: I am not going to comment
much on the speeches from the Government si de of the House, except to say that a
vindictive, nasty, petty little speech like the one Simon Bridges gave indicates to
everybody over here that he is not going anyw here near Cabinet and should go straight
back to Tauranga. We have seen some good speeches today, actua lly, from the other
side of the House. Mr Bridges did not give one of those.
I want to acknowledge all of the people who support us in our work here in
Parliament. Other speakers have gone th rough the list. Everybody who works in this
House works on behalf of all MPs to make th is place a better place to work, and I thank
them for all of the support that they give us.
I particularly want to acknowledge our sta ff outside Parliament, and that is for MPs
right across the House. Our st aff outside Parliament often put up with a lot of stress,
7500 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 12 Dec 2012
meet people who are in a very stressed state,  and do an incredible job for us in trying
circumstances. I thank all of those people.
I also want to acknowledge the families of MPs. It is only us and our partners and
our families who understand the pressure and st ress that go with being a member of
Parliament. Our families put up with a huge am ount, day in, day out, y ear in, year out,
and on behalf of the Labour Party I want to  acknowledge all of th e families, spouses,
partners, and those who suppor t MPs right across the Hous e. You do a tremendous job
for all of us.
David Shearer has already made clear that this has been a year to forget for the
Government and a year to forget for New Z ealand. I do want to acknowledge that for
many New Zealanders this will not be an eas y Christmas. For those who have lost their
jobs this year, or who have their jobs under th reat, this will be a difficult Christmas, and
we want to send our love and support from the Labour Party caucus.
Norman Kirk, I am told, once famously said: “New Zealanders have worked hard
this year. They deserve their Christmas.”, and it is in the spirit of Christmas that I
thought it might be appropriate  to run through the Nationa l Party’s “Twelve Days of
Christmas”. My colleagues know I cannot sing, but I am sure you will get the gist of the
tune as we go through the alternative to “The Twelve Days of Christmas”: “The Twelve
Fiascos of National”.
So for the first day of Christmas, Nati onal’s gift to Kiwi folk: John Banks on a
cabbage boat. The man with nothing to fear  and nothing to hide decided to hide
everything, and he fared very badly indee d. You have to have sympathy with John
Banks. I mean, who would remember taking a he licopter ride to a vast mansion to meet
an enormous German multimillionaire, who has got a giraffe, who then offers you
$50,000? I mean, it would not stick with me.
That gives us, I might say, our second fi asco. For the second day of Christmas,
National’s gift to Kiwi folk: two ch eques for $25,000, and John Banks on a cabbage
boat.
And 2012 has been the year for the National Government to insult people. Gerry
Brownlee tops the list for that, for telling Cantabrians, who were just trying to get on
with their lives, that they are carpers and moaners and declaring the major daily
newspaper in Christchurch as the enemy of  the recovery. But it is John Key who got
right into the insults this year. Red shirts are apparently gay, but there was no problem
with that, he told us, because by “gay” he m eant “weird”. Well, from this “weirdo” to
the PM, my message is: “You’re not a 15-year-old boy. Grow up.”
The Government moved on from insulting pe ople to insulting whole countries. The
UK press was less than impressed when the Prime Minister insulted David Beckham.
But the most ridiculous thi ng was that he could not even  get the insult right. When you
call people thick, it is pig excrement. When you are talking about bat excrement, it is
boring, as in “When Colin King speaks in Par liament, it is as boring as batshit.” The
well-known statesman John Key—[ Interruption]—keep up, keep up—said that
Hungarians do not go out at night in Afgha nistan, and Gerry Br ownlee followed his
lead, declaring that the Finns were une ducated, unemployed murderers who do not
respect women. So for the third day of Chri stmas, National’s gift to Kiwi folk: three
insulted countries, two cheques for $25,000, and John Banks on a cabbage boat.
This year the Prime Minister had a lot of  trouble remembering things. If he had a
plan for the country, he could not remember that, and the job was really getting to him.
He could not remember the briefings from  the Government Comm unications Security
Bureau, he could not remember which way he voted on alcohol re form, he could not
remember the discussions with Skycity about  the convention centre, and he could not
12 Dec 2012 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 7501
remember discussing a loan for MediaWorks . So for the fourth day of Christmas,
National’s gift to Kiwi folk: four brain fades.
Then John Key told us his biggest disappointment this year was pushing thorough the
sale of State assets. Well, Tony Ryall must have been too dazzled by his own tie that
day to read the memo, because he keeps sayi ng that things are on tr ack and that delays
were to be expected. Despite the fact that no other country in the world is pursuing asset
sales, this Government blunders on rega rdless. The good news is that hundreds of
thousands of New Zealanders know that the Government is wrong a nd that it will be
selling off our future, and we have a tric ky referendum ahead for the Government. So
for the fifth day of Christmas, National’s gift to Kiwi folk: five assets a-selling.
And who can forget the gift of a dysfuncti onal, completely out of control ACC? It
had the full cast of National Party characters: Michelle Boag, the woman who gifted
John Key to New Zealand, started lurking in the background of TV shots. Meanwhile, a
host of other people actually were shot: John Judge, Ralph Stewart, John McLiskie, and,
of course, Nick Smith—the man who was de finitely not trying to influence Bronwyn
Pullar’s case when he wrote a letter on minist erial letterhead to that effect! The other
casualty, of course, was Judith Collins’ credibility. So where are we up to? For the sixth
day of Christmas, National’s gift  to Kiwi folk: six ACC casualt ies, five assets a-selling,
four brain fades, three insulted countries, two cheques for $25,000, and John Banks on a
cabbage boat.
On this side of the House we always kne w that once Steven J oyce got his hands on
the employment portfolio, the only way was up—up, that is, in terms of the number of
people unemployed. The curse of Bill English has returned, as well, as unemployment is
the highest it has been since the last time he was finance Minister . A Government with
its hands off the wheel has decided the people are to blame—the people who are
looking for jobs are to blame. Well, my advi ce to the Government is if you are looking
for someone to blame, look in the mirror.  So for the seventh day of Christmas,
National’s gift to Kiwi folk: 7.3 percent unemployment.
The year 2012 would not have been the year it has been without National’s
unplanned open government policy. It was not so much the opening of the books as the
distribution of them along Lambton Quay. Pa ula Bennett excelled herself with looking
cross at her department, while having told the Prime Minister she would be on top of the
whole thing. But she was not alone. There were  at least four ACC leaks, a couple from
the Inland Revenue Department, and an extra special one from the Ministry of Social
Development. So for the eighth day of Chri stmas, National’s gift to Kiwi folk: eight
leaks of personal details.
This year’s Budget will mostly be remembered for the genius suggestion that the best
thing that the Government could do for th e education of young people would be to
squeeze a few more kids into our classes and cut funding for technology. But in the
hurly-burly of that U-turn, it is easily fo rgotten what the big idea of the 2012 Budget
was. The big idea to grow the economy, to turbocharge the economy, was the taxing of
paper boys—that great contri bution from Peter Dunne, a man who has never found an
issue he did not want to be on both sides of . He got in there and he said: “Those damn
kids. They’re ripping us off. We’re going to stop them. We’re going to put them in their
place.” So for the ninth day of Christmas, Nati onal’s gift to Kiwi folk: nine paper boys
a-crying.
If there is one thing we can be sure of when it comes to a National Government it is
the familiar smell. And no, it is not, as my colleague Clayton Cosgrove would say, the
pie warmer in Gerry Brownlee’s office, but ra ther the stench of cronyism: jobs for the
boys and the girls of the blue brigade. Apparently, there is nothing wrong with the
Prime Minister’s electorate chair being on the board of New Zealand On Air. Let us list
7502 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 12 Dec 2012
my top 10: Stephen McElrea,  Paula Rebstock, Peter Kiel y, Richard Long, Katherine
Rich, and two electorate chairs, Roger So wry, Wayne Mapp, Kerry Prendergast—there
are so many more. But for the 10 th day of Christmas, Nationa l’s gift to Kiwi folk: 10
cronies conspiring.
Across the Public Service morale has reached an all-time low. Over at the Ministry
of Foreign Affairs and Trade, a ministry th at prided itself on professionalism, it has
been picked apart by a Minister who has overseen the worst restructuring ever. The
leaks just keep on coming and we thank Murray McCully for that. So for the 11th day of
Christmas, National’s gift to Kiwi folk: 11 diplomats a-leaking.
So, on the 12 th of the 12 th, what is left for the 12 th fiasco? There are so many
candidates. Tim Groser is very familiar w ith the number 12, as th at is the number of
disciples he believed he had at the Worl d Trade Organization. Twelve is also the
number of times John Key has asked David Ca rter to be Speaker, and he still does not
want to do it. But there can be only one winner. From the portfolio where National’s
incompetence has been matched by its ignoran ce—from untrained teachers in charter
schools to Novopay being “no one paid”, to illegally closing special schools, and to
telling a fragile Christchurch community that  it would be losing its schools—these are
the stuff-ups of Hekia Parata.
So here we go. For “The Twelve Fiascos of  National” this year, National’s gift to

items.speaker: Kiwis are
items.text: 12 Hekia stuff-ups, 11 diplomats a-leaking, 10 cronies conspiring, nine paper
boys a-crying, eight leaks of personal deta ils, 7.3 percent unemployment, six ACC
casualties, five assets a-sell ing, four brain fades, three in sulted countries, two cheques
for $25,000, and John Banks on a cabbage boat.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: At the moment I am reading the
autobiography of the former British Prim e Minister Tony Blai r, and I was very
interested to note a quote he made about the Labour Party, which goes thus: “Today it
seems completely unacceptable, ridiculous even, that the uni ons played such a decisive
role in the selection of candidates and l eader … [Labour] was formed, funded, and run
by the unions, so the roots were inseparabl y intertwined, with, I’m afraid, very mixed
long-term consequences.” Well, I think he re ally got that right. I read it over the
weekend that the New Zealand Labour Party changed its constitution to do just that. I
can imagine the terror in David Shearer as he  realised that only 40 percent of his caucus
would be required by Mr Cunliffe to roll  him. I can imagine him running to David
Parker, his erstwhile finance spokesman, a nd saying: “David, you’re a finance guy.
What’s 40 percent of the caucus?”. And David Parker would turn around and go:
“David, it’s 95.” Shearer: “But, David, are you sure?”. Parker: “Y es, I’ve checked it
twice.” Shearer: “But ha ng on, there’s only 34 in our caucus.” Parker: “No, it’s
definitely 95.”
The most amazing thing about last week was the fact that when the results of one
poll that might have suggested  that the tide was turning—a nd I suggest that that was
pretty premature—had the Greens measuring up the hemp curtains in the Beehive, Mr
Shearer immediately ruled out Dr Russel Norman  as a future Minister of Finance. Well,
I think that is a bit dodgy, really, because he might be crazy, but at least he can count. It
is one of the prerequisites for being a Mini ster of Finance. Even Mr Parker in his
speech, in the biggest suck-up of the day, said  he gave Mr Shearer  7 to 11 out of 10.
How on earth one gets 7 to 11 out of 10 fo r a performance by the Leader of the
Opposition I will never know.

items.speaker: But I say this to the Greens
items.text: if one wants to eliminate child poverty, do not give me a
family support payment. It is not going to work. It needs to be more targeted. To Gareth

items.speaker: Hughes
items.text: if one calls for an  inquiry into a method of mining and drilling, and the
Parliamentary Commissioner for the Envir onment comes out and says there is no
12 Dec 2012 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 7503
evidence that it is unsafe,  then listen to the Parlia mentary Commissioner. Do not
continue to bury one’s head in the sand, becau se that is all we ha ve heard from Labour
and the Greens this year. If only we coul d hear one word—one word. That word is
“Yes”: yes, we support something that the Government is doing to grow the economy.
But, no, they say no to  the intensification of  the agricultural sect or, no to more oil and
gas exploration, and no to more good jobs coming from Australia to New Zealand.
Making welfare work, the 90-day probation pe riod, any of our labour market reforms,
ultra-fast broadband, foreign investment in  New Zealand, and the 3,000 jobs that came
from The Hobbit—no, no, no.
Well, I know why the polls are showing that the Government  support has not
flinched in 4 years. It is because this is a caucus united behind a leader. I want to thank
my colleagues for their support through this year . It has made my job easier as senior
whip. The fact is that the energy is hi gh, the discipline is good, and we are united
behind the Prime Minister as leader of this  party. Those are some lessons that I think
Opposition parties could draw on. But I also want  to add my thanks to the staff, as has
been mentioned by other colleagues: securit y, Hansard, the Clerks, and the many others
who make Parliament work. I also want to acknowledge my fellow whips. There is a lot
that goes on behind the scenes that is not seen, and I have  enjoyed working with Messrs
Hipkins, Hughes, Stuart, and Flavell, and Ms Fenton.
But to you, Mr Speaker, call me Nostradamus-like, but I have a feeling that there will
be an opportunity in the not too distant future  for some teary-eyed nostalgia. But in the
meantime, on behalf of my caucus, I do wa nt to congratulate you on, and thank you for,
the manner in which you, your deputy, and your assistants have managed proceedings in
the House this year. To you, merry Christmas. Enjoy a safe and relaxing break. Also to
members of the public and all in this Hous e, a very merry Christmas and a happy and
more prosperous New Year.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: My colleagues, thank you very much for your kind comments in
respect of me and my team of Speakers—my excellent deputy, Eric Roy, and assistants
Lindsay Tisch and Ross Robertson. They do a very committed job, and it is much
appreciated. Can I also th ank you for the kind support yo u gave all the people who
make this place operate on our behalf, because  there are so many of them and they do
such a wonderful job for us.
I think one of the notable features of th is year has been the impact of the new
Standing Orders. It is interesting that in the last parliamentary term—the 49 th
Parliament—a quarter of our sitting hours was under urgency. This year we have sat for
a total of 543 hours, 9½ of which were under urgency—that is less than 2 percent. We
sat 35½ hours of extended sittings, but that is a much more measured way of advancing
the legislative programme. It meant that le gislation with wide support across the House
could be facilitated, enabling much more fo cus on areas of difference and areas of
controversy. I think the Bu siness Committee used the ne w Standing Orders very
effectively, and I want to congratulate the Business Committee, and, in particular, the
Leader of the House, the Hon Gerry Brownl ee, and also the shadow Leader of the
House, the Hon Trevor Mallard.
I think the new Standing Orders covering me mbers’ bills have also been pretty
successful. In 2011 we had no members’ bills in troduced into the House; this year there
have been 34. That is a huge improvement in  the opportunity for members to have their
proposals considered by the House.
The changes in the Standing Orders also provided for referral to select committees of
bills, where the period of referral was less than 4 months, to be a debatable motion
without time limit. It is interesting the impact that has had. In 2011, 13 bills were
referred to select committees with a report-back date of less than 4 months. This year
7504 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 12 Dec 2012
only seven bills had a report-back date of less than 4 months. So there has been almost a
halving of referral for a short period of tim e, which must be good for the ability for the
public to have greater input into our legislative programme.
All together, I think the changes s how that the House can make gradual
improvement to its operations. So members of the Standing Orders Committee of the
49th Parliament, who did so much work on those changes, I think should be
congratulated on the effort made and the thought that went into them.
This year has been a year of consistent  work in the House: 125 bills received the
Royal assent, five are waiting for that, 1,100 oral questions were answered, and only
two members were yellow-carded. A total of fi ve, I think, have been yellow-carded in
my 4 years as the Speaker, and I think that is  something of a recor d, because I think in
the old days that would have been about the norm on 1 day.
One of the gems in the House this year passed right over me. I missed totally when
Gerry Brownlee said, in answer to a suppl ementary question from Phil Twyford on my
left, with an absolutely deadpan face, that  the Government would consider hiring Lyle
Lanley and associates to scope the city rail link, referring to the good work they had
done on similar projects in Brockway, Ogde nville, and North Haverbrook. I thought it
was an unusual answer, I must say, but I di d not click that Mr Brownlee was into The
Simpsons and “Marge vs. the Monorail”. I guess what it means is I am getting old and it
is almost time to go.
Colleagues, I am conscious that this is the last time I will speak to you in the
adjournment debate, and I want to take th is opportunity to particularly thank the
General Manager of the Parliamentary Servi ce. The general manager carries out quite a
thankless task, and I think he does it with great commitment, and I want to express
appreciation for the work he has done.
I want to pay particular trib ute to our outstanding Clerk of the House, Mary Harris,
and her team in the Clerk’s Office, including her gem of an executive assistant, Andie
Lindsay. It is such a privilege to work with these two, and, Mary, I cannot express
sufficient thanks for the wonderful job you do.
To my team in the Speaker’s office, and especially my senior private secretary, Beryl
Bright, again I want to pass on huge thanks. We now run the protocol and reception area
in the Speaker’s office, on one-third of the co st it used to cost taxpayers. That is a
challenge to Ministers and Government departments—we run my department there now
on a third, not one third less but a third, of wh at it once cost. I am not sure it runs that
much worse. My senior private secr etary, Beryl Bright, is now in her 27 th year of
looking after me, and goodness knows what kind of  cruel punishment that is, but I want
to thank her hugely.
Colleagues, do have a great Christmas. En joy your break away from this place. I
think only those who have been here know how much this place can be a drain on your
private lives. Through you, can I pass on my th anks to your spouses, your partners, and
your families for all they give up to suppor t you in this work. Enjoy your Christmas
with your families. Go well.
Motion agreed to.
The House adjourned at 5.33 p.m.

WEDNESDAY, 12 DECEMBER 2012 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Economic Programme—Progress 
1. TODD McCLAY (National—Rotorua)  to the Minister of Finance : What 
progress has the Government made with its economic programme in 2012? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associ ate Minister of Finance) on behalf of the Minister 
of Finance : The Government is making very good progress in the face of very 
significant ongoing global economic challenges. The Government was re-elected with a 
clear plan to build a faster -growing economy that can enc ourage businesses to invest 
and grow. We are focused on four main  priorities: responsibly manage the 
Government’s finances so we can return to  surplus and repay debt, push ahead with a 
wide-ranging programme of microeconomic re form to create a more productive and 
competitive economy, drive better results and better value from public services, and 
support the rebuild of our second -largest city after its eart hquakes. New Zealanders can 
be reassured that this Government is abso lutely focused on creating more opportunities 
to grow the economy, unlike the Greens-Labour Opposition, which is constantly— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! Order! 
Todd McClay: What progress is the Government making with responsibly managing 
its finances so it can return to surplus, start repaying debt, and build a buffer against 
future shocks? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE: Once again, the Government is making very good progress. 
On coming into office in late 2008, the Government was presented with forecasts 
showing permanent structural deficits a nd ever-increasing Government debt. This 
Government has worked hard to turn that  situation round by reining in new spending 
and reprioritising existing spending to deliver better results, and that is all despite the 
extra costs that have come from the Ca nterbury earthquakes. The Crown’s operating 
deficit before gains and losses was $9.2 billion in the year ended June 2012—half of the 
$18.4 billion in the previous year—and the late st forecast will be included in the Half 
Year Economic and Fiscal Update next Tues day. The Government ha s set a target of 
returning to surplus in 2014-15. That is very important so that we can reduce debt to 
more prudent levels and build resilience to future shocks. 
Todd McClay : What approach is the Governme nt taking in building a more 
productive and competitive economy? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : The Government is working aggressively to do everything 
to give businesses the confid ence to invest, grow, and crea te jobs. The Government has 
taken a wide range of measures to ensure economic growth is built on a solid foundation 
of exports, savings, and productive investment. The programme that we are undertaking 
is set out in the Business Growth Agenda, which contains more than 250 initiatives for 
expanding our export markets, encouragi ng innovation, developing skills, building 
infrastructure, improving our natural resour ce use, and growi ng capital markets. 
Together they are a comprehensive agenda  of microeconomic reform, which will 
support jobs and assist businesses to become more internationally competitive. 
Mr SPEAKER : Before I call the honourable memb er, the House is unacceptably 
noisy. But I remind Ministers that if they go on with very long answers—[ Interruption] 
Order! If they go on with very long answers the House will tend to get restive. 
7456 Questions for Oral Answer 12 Dec 2012 
Todd McClay: What reports has he received on  proposals that would put the New 
Zealand economy at risk, cost thousands  of jobs, and increase the country’s 
vulnerability to overseas lenders? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : I have seen many such propos als this year. They include

Where will you go these holidays? Are you lucky enough to have a bach that is close 
to the sea somewhere, a place that you and yo ur family have been going to now year 
after year after year, for as far back as you can remember? Or maybe you have a 
favourite motor camp to stay at—the kind of place where you have to muck in with 
other families from all over the country, pitching your tents, peeling the spuds, herding 
the tribes of children, and all done to the soundtrack  of the cricket th at is playing on 
your neighbour’s radio.  
The Kiwi summer holidays are something pr etty special, especially when you are a 
kid. You can escape those pesky grown-ups a nd go on an adventure, often with a brand 
new, day-old bestest friend ever. Those long, hot summer days seem to stretch on for 
ever and ever until you can hardly keep your eyes open, and then before you know it 
you are asleep to the sound of the moreporks calling. But then the new day breaks, cool 
and full of potential, and you get another chance to master your skateboard or go fishing 
for kai moana with your nanny and your koro a nd your cousins, or you are being asked, 
yet again, to go and search for that extra c up of flour to help your mother, who has run 
7474 Adjournment & Sitting Programme 12 Dec 2012 
out for making her cake that day. These are the kinds of moments that we live for and 
work hard to provide for our children and the children of our friends and our 
neighbours. This is what Christmas is for ma ny of us, and this is what makes us truly 
rich as New Zealanders.  
But this is not the Christmas story fo r an increasing number of New Zealand’s 
children, and it was not mine. I had a lot of freedom as a child in the summer holidays, 
but we did not get to go away. Most of my holidays were spent wandering around those 
dry, grassy paddocks of Ashhurst , dodging the thistles in our bare feet , trying not to get 
electrocuted by the farmer’s fences, and waiting for our dad to come home from a day at 
work so he could take us all down to the river for a swim.  
Those were some of the best times of my summer holidays. We would mob our dad 
when he drove up the driveway. Then there was the ride down to the river on the back 
of his Holden Kingswood—can you remember  those—with the door down and our legs 
hanging off the edge so that we could jump off and be the first to race to the cold, cold 
water. My cousins and I, and my friends, and anyone else who was around would join in 
to spend our evenings there doing dive-bom bs off the bank of the river, hunting for 
bullies and for freshwater crays, and squealing about the eels that might come out and 
bite us on the bum, and all under the watchful  eye of our dad, who was usually having a 
good wash after a hard day’s work at the bread factory.  
Our swimming hole at the Pohangina River was our place to forget about everything. 
Down there it did not matter whether you were rich or poor, Māori or Pākehā, a boy or a 
girl. The river brought us all together, and it gave us some of the happiest moments of 
our childhood. We did not have  much, but I did have a wh ānau who loved and nurtured 
me in a country that made sure that I had enough to eat, a good school to go to, and a 
safe, clean river that I could spend my summer holidays swimming in.  
That is a country to love. Th at is a country to fight for— a country that protects its 
vulnerable, loves its beautiful environment, and empowers all of its children, rich or 
poor, M āori or P ākehā, boy or girl, to become the best that they can be. That is a 
country I want my kids and grandkids to grow  up in, and I want my neighbours’ kids to 
grow up in it too, no ma tter who they are. I be lieve that this is a vision that we can 
achieve only if we work together. I believe that this is actually the only way to live with 
dignity and grace in this country. I believe that  this is what we, as  New Zealanders, in 
our modest ways quietly yearn for.  
But our lucky country is s lipping away from us from  right under our feet. Our 
country has never been wealthier, yet the swimming hole of my childhood is now at risk 
of being too polluted and unsafe to swim in, just like more than half of our lowland 
rivers that are already so polluted. Our count ry has never been w ealthier, but we are 
living at a time when the differences between us have never been wider. We are rapidly 
becoming one of the most unequal countries  in the developed world, where once we 
were one of the most equal.  
Our country has never been w ealthier, but it is hard to remember a time when it was 
so difficult to find an ordinary job that  paid a decent wage—enough to save up some 
money and to be able to afford to take the kids away on holiday this Christmas. It is like 
we have forgotten what it is like to sta nd alongside one anothe r and remind ourselves 
that we are each our sister’s and our brother’ s keeper. But it does not have to be this 
way if we choose to live with compassion and generosity—in the spirit of Christmas, no

Mr SPEAKER : My colleagues, thank you very much for your kind comments in 
respect of me and my team of Speakers—my excellent deputy, Eric Roy, and assistants 
Lindsay Tisch and Ross Robertson. They do a very committed job, and it is much 
appreciated. Can I also th ank you for the kind support yo u gave all the people who 
make this place operate on our behalf, because  there are so many of them and they do 
such a wonderful job for us. 
I think one of the notable features of th is year has been the impact of the new 
Standing Orders. It is interesting that in the last parliamentary term—the 49 th 
Parliament—a quarter of our sitting hours was under urgency. This year we have sat for 
a total of 543 hours, 9½ of which were under urgency—that is less than 2 percent. We 
sat 35½ hours of extended sittings, but that is a much more measured way of advancing 
the legislative programme. It meant that le gislation with wide support across the House 
could be facilitated, enabling much more fo cus on areas of difference and areas of 
controversy. I think the Bu siness Committee used the ne w Standing Orders very 
effectively, and I want to congratulate the Business Committee, and, in particular, the 
Leader of the House, the Hon Gerry Brownl ee, and also the shadow Leader of the 
House, the Hon Trevor Mallard. 
I think the new Standing Orders covering me mbers’ bills have also been pretty 
successful. In 2011 we had no members’ bills in troduced into the House; this year there 
have been 34. That is a huge improvement in  the opportunity for members to have their 
proposals considered by the House. 
The changes in the Standing Orders also provided for referral to select committees of 
bills, where the period of referral was less than 4 months, to be a debatable motion 
without time limit. It is interesting the impact that has had. In 2011, 13 bills were 
referred to select committees with a report-back date of less than 4 months. This year

only seven bills had a report-back date of less than 4 months. So there has been almost a 
halving of referral for a short period of tim e, which must be good for the ability for the 
public to have greater input into our legislative programme. 
 All together, I think the changes s how that the House can make gradual 
improvement to its operations. So members of the Standing Orders Committee of the 
49th Parliament, who did so much work on those changes, I think should be 
congratulated on the effort made and the thought that went into them. 
This year has been a year of consistent  work in the House: 125 bills received the 
Royal assent, five are waiting for that, 1,100 oral questions were answered, and only 
two members were yellow-carded. A total of fi ve, I think, have been yellow-carded in 
my 4 years as the Speaker, and I think that is  something of a recor d, because I think in 
the old days that would have been about the norm on 1 day. 
One of the gems in the House this year passed right over me. I missed totally when 
Gerry Brownlee said, in answer to a suppl ementary question from Phil Twyford on my 
left, with an absolutely deadpan face, that  the Government would consider hiring Lyle 
Lanley and associates to scope the city rail link, referring to the good work they had 
done on similar projects in Brockway, Ogde nville, and North Haverbrook. I thought it 
was an unusual answer, I must say, but I di d not click that Mr Brownlee was into The 
Simpsons and “Marge vs. the Monorail”. I guess what it means is I am getting old and it 
is almost time to go. 
Colleagues, I am conscious that this is the last time I will speak to you in the 
adjournment debate, and I want to take th is opportunity to particularly thank the 
General Manager of the Parliamentary Servi ce. The general manager carries out quite a 
thankless task, and I think he does it with great commitment, and I want to express 
appreciation for the work he has done. 
I want to pay particular trib ute to our outstanding Clerk of the House, Mary Harris, 
and her team in the Clerk’s Office, including her gem of an executive assistant, Andie 
Lindsay. It is such a privilege to work with these two, and, Mary, I cannot express 
sufficient thanks for the wonderful job you do. 
To my team in the Speaker’s office, and especially my senior private secretary, Beryl 
Bright, again I want to pass on huge thanks. We now run the protocol and reception area 
in the Speaker’s office, on one-third of the co st it used to cost taxpayers. That is a 
challenge to Ministers and Government departments—we run my department there now 
on a third, not one third less but a third, of wh at it once cost. I am not sure it runs that 
much worse. My senior private secr etary, Beryl Bright, is now in her 27 th year of 
looking after me, and goodness knows what kind of  cruel punishment that is, but I want 
to thank her hugely. 
Colleagues, do have a great Christmas. En joy your break away from this place. I 
think only those who have been here know how much this place can be a drain on your 
private lives. Through you, can I pass on my th anks to your spouses, your partners, and 
your families for all they give up to suppor t you in this work. Enjoy your Christmas 
with your families. Go well.
